questions.q: Real GDP has declined for two straight quarters, factory orders are shrinking and unemployment claims keep climbing. Which phase of the business cycle best describes this economy?
options: Expansion
Peak
Recovery
Contraction
questions.explain: Falling output combined with rising unemployment marks a contraction, the downward leg of the cycle. A peak is the turning point at the top, when activity stops rising; it is not a period of sustained decline. Expansion and recovery describe growing output.

questions.q: An economist wants a statistic that tends to turn up or down BEFORE the overall economy does. Which of the following is generally classified as a leading indicator?
options: Average duration of unemployment
Industrial production
Building permits for new private housing
Personal income excluding transfer payments
questions.explain: Permits are issued before construction begins, so they signal future activity and are a classic leading indicator. Industrial production and personal income move with the economy (coincident). The average duration of unemployment changes after the cycle has already turned, so it is a lagging indicator.

questions.q: Which economic statistic is usually classified as a lagging indicator, confirming a turn in the economy only after it has occurred?
options: Stock prices of large companies
The average prime rate charged by banks
Average weekly hours worked in manufacturing
New orders for consumer goods
questions.explain: Banks adjust the prime rate after economic conditions and monetary policy have already shifted, so it lags the cycle. Stock prices, factory hours and new orders all tend to change ahead of the broader economy and are treated as leading indicators.

questions.q: The Federal Reserve wants to slow an economy where inflation is running well above its target. Which open market action is consistent with that goal?
options: Selling Treasury securities to banks and dealers
Buying Treasury securities from banks and dealers
Lowering the discount rate
Reducing interest paid on bank reserves
questions.explain: When the Fed sells Treasuries, buyers pay with reserves, which drains money from the banking system and pushes short-term rates up, a restrictive move. Buying securities, cutting the discount rate or paying less on reserves would all loosen credit, which is the opposite of what fighting inflation requires.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of expansionary FISCAL policy?
options: The Federal Reserve buys long-term Treasury bonds
Congress raises individual income tax rates
The Federal Reserve lowers its federal funds rate target
Congress passes a bill increasing federal spending on highways
questions.explain: Fiscal policy is government taxing and spending, set by Congress and the President. More government spending adds to demand, so it is expansionary. The Fed's bond purchases and rate cuts are expansionary too, but they are monetary policy, not fiscal. Raising taxes is a contractionary fiscal move.

questions.q: Yields on 3-month Treasury bills are higher than yields on 10-year Treasury notes. How is this yield curve described, and what is it often taken to signal?
options: Normal; it signals strong future growth
Flat; it signals that inflation is rising quickly
Inverted; many analysts view it as a warning of a possible slowdown
Inverted; it signals that long-term inflation expectations are rising
questions.explain: When short maturities yield more than long maturities the curve is inverted. Markets are pricing in lower future short-term rates, which usually happens when investors expect the economy to weaken. Rising long-term inflation expectations would push long yields up and steepen the curve, the opposite of an inversion.

questions.q: Under normal conditions the Treasury yield curve slopes upward. Which explanation best accounts for that shape?
options: Short-term securities carry more default risk than long-term ones
Investors require extra compensation for tying up money longer and bearing more interest rate risk
The Federal Reserve sets long-term rates above short-term rates by law
Long-term bonds are more liquid than short-term bills
questions.explain: Lenders who commit money for longer periods face more uncertainty about inflation and rates, so they demand a higher yield. Default risk is the same for all Treasury maturities, the Fed does not fix long-term rates by law, and short-term bills are generally more liquid than long bonds.

questions.q: Over several months the gap between yields on BB-rated corporate bonds and comparable Treasury securities widens sharply. What does this most likely indicate?
options: Investors are demanding more compensation for default risk, often a sign of economic worry
Investors expect corporate defaults to fall
Treasury securities have become riskier than corporate bonds
Inflation expectations have dropped to zero
questions.explain: The credit spread is the extra yield over Treasuries that compensates for default risk. A widening spread means investors want more reward for that risk, which usually reflects concern about the economy or corporate earnings. Expecting fewer defaults would narrow the spread, not widen it.

questions.q: A U.S. investor buys shares of a German company. A year later the share price in euros is unchanged, but the euro has risen 8% against the U.S. dollar. Ignoring dividends, what is the investor's approximate return in dollars?
options: A loss of about 8%
It cannot be positive because the share price did not change
A gain of about 8%
questions.explain: The shares are worth the same number of euros, but each euro now buys about 8% more dollars, so the position is worth about 8% more in dollar terms. A rising foreign currency adds to a U.S. investor's return; a falling one would subtract from it. That is currency (exchange rate) risk working in the investor's favor.

questions.q: Which transaction is recorded in the CURRENT account of the U.S. balance of payments?
options: A U.S. resident's purchase of shares listed in Tokyo
A foreign company's purchase of a factory in Ohio
A U.S. manufacturer's sale of machinery to a buyer in Brazil
A foreign central bank's purchase of U.S. Treasury bonds
questions.explain: The current account tracks trade in goods and services plus income and transfer flows, so an export of machinery belongs there. Purchases of stocks, factories or bonds across borders are investments in assets and are recorded in the financial (capital) account, not the current account.

questions.q: Prices across the economy fall steadily for two years, which nobody expected. Which group is generally hurt the most?
options: Lenders holding fixed-rate loans
Borrowers with fixed-rate debt
Holders of cash
Retirees receiving fixed pension payments
questions.explain: In deflation, money gains purchasing power. Borrowers must repay fixed amounts with dollars that are worth more than when they borrowed, so the real burden of their debt grows. Lenders, cash holders and people on fixed incomes all benefit because their fixed dollars buy more.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the Consumer Price Index (CPI)?
options: It measures changes over time in the prices urban consumers pay for a market basket of goods and services
It measures the total value of goods and services produced in the U.S.
It measures prices received by domestic producers for their output
It measures the percentage of the labor force that is unemployed
questions.explain: The CPI, published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, follows the cost of a fixed basket of consumer goods and services and is the most widely cited inflation gauge. Total output is GDP, and prices received by producers are measured by the Producer Price Index, a different series.

questions.q: Gross domestic product (GDP) is best defined as:
options: The total income earned by a country's citizens anywhere in the world
The value of all goods sold, including intermediate goods used in production
Exports minus imports during a year
The market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a period
questions.explain: GDP counts final goods and services produced inside the country, whoever owns the factors of production. Counting intermediate goods would double count output. Income earned by citizens worldwide is closer to gross national product, and exports minus imports is only the net export component of GDP.

questions.q: A country's government has issued large amounts of debt and investors begin to doubt it can repay. Which outcome is most likely for that government's bonds?
options: Their yields fall and their prices rise
Their prices rise because supply increases
Their yields rise and their prices fall
Nothing changes because government bonds have no default risk
questions.explain: Sovereign debt is not free of default risk. When investors fear a government may not pay, they demand a higher yield, and because bond prices move opposite to yields, prices fall. The belief that all government bonds are riskless is the trap; even large countries have restructured debt.

questions.q: Which financial statement reports a company's assets, liabilities and shareholders' equity at a single point in time?
options: Income statement (profit and loss)
Balance sheet
Statement of cash flows
Statement of retained earnings
questions.explain: The balance sheet is a snapshot on a specific date, and assets always equal liabilities plus equity. The income statement and the statement of cash flows cover a period of time, such as a quarter or a year, rather than a single date.

questions.q: A consulting firm finishes a project in December and is paid by the client in February. Under accrual accounting, when is the revenue recorded?
options: In December, when it was earned
In February, when cash is received
Half in December and half in February
Only after the annual audit
questions.explain: Accrual accounting recognizes revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, regardless of when cash changes hands. Recording the revenue in February, when the payment arrives, describes cash-basis accounting, which most public companies do not use for financial reporting.

questions.q: On a company's statement of cash flows, in which section does the payment of cash dividends to shareholders appear?
options: Operating activities
Investing activities
It does not appear because dividends are not an expense
Financing activities
questions.explain: Transactions with owners and lenders, such as paying dividends, issuing stock or repaying debt, are financing activities. Investing activities cover buying and selling long-term assets, and operating activities cover day-to-day business. Dividends are not on the income statement, but they do use cash and appear on this statement.

questions.q: An independent auditor issues an unqualified (clean) opinion on a company's annual financial statements. What does this mean?
options: The company is guaranteed to remain profitable
The auditor found and corrected every error, however small
The statements present the company's financial position fairly in all material respects under the applicable accounting framework
The SEC has approved the company's statements
questions.explain: A clean opinion is the auditor's view that the statements are fairly presented in all material respects. It is not a guarantee of future results, it does not mean that no immaterial errors exist, and the SEC does not approve or certify a company's financial statements.

questions.q: A public company must promptly disclose an unscheduled material event, such as the sudden departure of its chief executive. Which SEC filing is generally used?
options: Form 10-K
Form 8-K
Form 10-Q
Form ADV
questions.explain: Form 8-K is the current report companies file for significant events between periodic reports. Form 10-K is the annual report and Form 10-Q the quarterly report. Form ADV is the registration form for investment advisers, not for operating companies.

questions.q: Which type of risk CANNOT be reduced by adding more stocks from different industries to a portfolio?
options: Market (systematic) risk
Business risk of a single company
Risk of a product recall at one firm
Management risk at one company
questions.explain: Systematic risk comes from forces that affect the whole market, such as recessions or interest rate changes, so diversification cannot remove it. Business, recall and management risks are specific to one company (unsystematic) and shrink as a portfolio holds more unrelated issuers.

questions.q: A client keeps $50,000 in a checking account that pays no interest while 1-year Treasury bills yield 4%. What is the approximate annual opportunity cost of this choice?
options: $0, because the money is safe
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the return given up by not choosing the next best alternative. Leaving $50,000 idle instead of earning 4% gives up $50,000 x 0.04 = $2,000 a year. Saying the cost is zero because the account is safe confuses opportunity cost with risk of loss.

questions.q: A corporation is liquidated. Which group is normally paid LAST from the remaining assets?
options: Preferred stockholders
Holders of subordinated debentures
Common stockholders
Secured bondholders
questions.explain: Creditors come before owners. Secured creditors are paid first from their collateral, then unsecured and subordinated debt holders, then preferred stockholders. Common stockholders hold the residual claim and receive only what is left, often nothing. Preferred stock ranks ahead of common but behind all debt.

questions.q: Which investment, if held to maturity, carries NO reinvestment risk?
options: A 30-year Treasury bond
A zero-coupon Treasury STRIP
A callable corporate bond
A mortgage-backed pass-through security
questions.explain: Reinvestment risk is the chance that interim cash flows must be reinvested at lower rates. A zero-coupon security makes no payments until maturity, so there is nothing to reinvest. Coupon bonds pay interest along the way, callable bonds may be redeemed early, and mortgage pools return principal through prepayments.

questions.q: Which client is MOST exposed to purchasing power (inflation) risk?
options: A retiree living on a fixed annuity payment that never changes
A worker whose salary is adjusted for cost of living each year
An investor holding Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities
A homeowner with a fixed-rate mortgage
questions.explain: Inflation erodes what a fixed payment can buy, so someone depending on a level annuity bears the full impact. Cost-of-living raises and TIPS adjust upward with inflation, and a fixed-rate borrower actually benefits because the debt is repaid with cheaper dollars.

questions.q: A company has current assets of $600,000 and current liabilities of $300,000. What is its current ratio?
questions.explain: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities = $600,000 / $300,000 = 2.0. It is a liquidity measure showing the company has $2 of short-term assets for each $1 of short-term obligations. $300,000 is working capital (the difference), not the ratio.

questions.q: A company reports current assets of $600,000, of which $200,000 is inventory, and current liabilities of $250,000. What is its quick (acid-test) ratio?
questions.explain: The quick ratio removes inventory, the least liquid current asset: ($600,000 - $200,000) / $250,000 = $400,000 / $250,000 = 1.6. Using all current assets gives 2.4, which is the current ratio and the most tempting wrong answer.

questions.q: A firm has total debt of $4 million and shareholders' equity of $8 million. What is its debt-to-equity ratio?
questions.explain: Debt-to-equity = total debt / shareholders' equity = $4 million / $8 million = 0.5. It measures financial leverage. Dividing equity by debt gives 2.0, the inverse, and dividing debt by total capital ($12 million) gives 0.33, a different ratio.

questions.q: A stock trades at $60 and the company earned $4 per share over the past year. What is its price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio?
questions.explain: P/E = market price per share / earnings per share = $60 / $4 = 15. Investors are paying $15 for each $1 of annual earnings. Dividing earnings by price (4 / 60 = 6.7%) gives the earnings yield, the inverse of the P/E.

questions.q: A stock trades at $30 per share and its book value per share is $20. What is its price-to-book ratio, and how might a value investor view it?
options: 0.67; a ratio below 1 always means the stock is overvalued
1.5; a higher price-to-book is generally associated with value stocks
10; the difference between price and book value
1.5; a lower price-to-book is generally associated with value stocks
questions.explain: Price-to-book = $30 / $20 = 1.5. Value investors look for stocks priced low relative to assets or earnings, so lower price-to-book ratios tend to mark value stocks, while growth stocks usually carry higher ratios. The $10 difference is not a ratio.

questions.q: A company pays an annual dividend of $1.20 per share and earned $4.00 per share. What is its dividend payout ratio?
questions.explain: Payout ratio = dividends per share / earnings per share = $1.20 / $4.00 = 30%. The other 70% of earnings is retained in the business, which is the retention ratio and the trap answer. Dividend yield would instead divide the dividend by the share price.

questions.q: An investor deposits $10,000 in an account earning 5% compounded annually. Assuming no withdrawals, how much will the account hold after 2 years?
questions.explain: Future value = $10,000 x 1.05 x 1.05 = $11,025. In year two interest is earned on the first year's interest ($10,500 x 5% = $525). Simple interest would give only $11,000, which ignores compounding.

questions.q: An investor will receive $11,000 one year from today. If the appropriate discount rate is 10%, what is the present value of that payment?
questions.explain: Present value = future value / (1 + rate) = $11,000 / 1.10 = $10,000. Subtracting 10% of $11,000 gives $9,900, a common mistake that discounts the wrong base. $12,100 compounds forward instead of discounting back.

questions.q: A project's cash flows are discounted at the firm's required rate of return and the net present value (NPV) comes to +$250,000. What does this indicate?
options: The project's internal rate of return is below the required rate
The project will lose $250,000
The project's payback period is exactly one year
The project is expected to earn more than the required rate of return
questions.explain: NPV is the present value of future cash flows minus the cost. A positive NPV means the project adds value at the chosen discount rate, which also means its internal rate of return exceeds that rate. A negative NPV would signal the opposite.

questions.q: Which statement correctly defines the internal rate of return (IRR) of an investment?
options: The average annual cash flow divided by the initial cost
The rate of return required by the investor
The discount rate at which the present value of future cash flows equals the initial cost, making NPV zero
The return earned after deducting inflation
questions.explain: IRR is the discount rate that sets net present value to zero. If it exceeds the investor's required return, the investment is attractive. The required return is a separate hurdle rate used for comparison, and the inflation-adjusted figure is a real return, not the IRR.

questions.q: A fund's annual returns over five years were 4%, 6%, 6%, 9% and 15%. What is the arithmetic mean return?
questions.explain: Mean = (4 + 6 + 6 + 9 + 15) / 5 = 40 / 5 = 8%. The median (middle value) and the mode (most frequent value) are both 6%, which is the trap. The 15% year pulls the mean above the median, showing how outliers affect the mean.

questions.q: A portfolio's yearly returns were -5%, 3%, 8%, 12% and 20%. What is the range of these returns?
options: 25 percentage points
20 percentage points
15 percentage points
7.6 percentage points
questions.explain: Range = highest value - lowest value = 20% - (-5%) = 25 percentage points. Forgetting that subtracting a negative number adds it leads to 15. The range is a simple dispersion measure that depends only on the two extreme observations.

questions.q: A fund has an expected annual return of 10% with a standard deviation of 6%. Assuming returns are normally distributed, roughly two-thirds of annual returns should fall within which range?
questions.explain: About 68% of outcomes lie within one standard deviation of the mean: 10% - 6% = 4% and 10% + 6% = 16%. Two standard deviations (-2% to 22%) would cover about 95%. Standard deviation measures total volatility around the average.

questions.q: A stock has a beta of 1.3. If the market rises 10%, what move would the beta suggest for the stock, all else equal?
options: A rise of about 7.7%
A rise of about 1.3%
A rise of about 13%
A fall of about 13%
questions.explain: Beta measures sensitivity to market movements. A beta of 1.3 implies the stock tends to move 1.3 times as much as the market: 10% x 1.3 = 13%. A beta below 1 would imply smaller moves, and a negative beta would imply moves opposite to the market.

questions.q: A manager's portfolio returned 12% last year. Based on its beta, the capital asset pricing model predicted a return of 10%. What is the portfolio's alpha?
options: Negative 2%
Positive 2%
Positive 12%
Positive 22%
questions.explain: Alpha = actual return - expected return = 12% - 10% = +2%. A positive alpha means the manager beat the return justified by the portfolio's market risk. A negative alpha would mean underperformance relative to that risk-adjusted expectation.

questions.q: Portfolio X returned 11% with a standard deviation of 16%; Portfolio Y returned 9% with a standard deviation of 8%. The risk-free rate is 3%. Which portfolio had the better Sharpe ratio?
options: Portfolio Y, at 0.75 versus 0.50
Portfolio X, at 0.50 versus 0.75
Portfolio X, because it had the higher return
They are equal
questions.explain: Sharpe ratio = (return - risk-free rate) / standard deviation. X: (11 - 3) / 16 = 0.50. Y: (9 - 3) / 8 = 0.75. Y earned more excess return per unit of total risk, even though X had the higher raw return, which is the trap.

questions.q: Two assets have a correlation coefficient of -1.0. What does this mean for a portfolio combining them?
options: Their returns move together exactly, offering no diversification benefit
Their returns are unrelated
Both assets will lose money
Their returns move in exactly opposite directions, offering the maximum possible diversification benefit
questions.explain: Correlation ranges from -1 to +1. Perfect negative correlation means one asset rises when the other falls in a fixed proportion, so combining them can cut volatility the most. A correlation of +1 gives no diversification benefit, and 0 means no linear relationship.

questions.q: Which measure shows how volatile a stock has been relative to the overall market rather than in absolute terms?
options: Standard deviation
Mean return
Beta
Range
questions.explain: Beta compares a security's movements with those of a market benchmark, so it captures systematic risk only. Standard deviation and range measure total variability of the security's own returns without reference to the market, and the mean is an average, not a risk measure.

questions.q: Using the rule of 72, about how long does it take an investment earning 8% compounded annually to double?
options: About 12.5 years
About 9 years
About 6 years
About 8 years
questions.explain: The rule of 72 estimates doubling time by dividing 72 by the annual rate: 72 / 8 = 9 years. Dividing 100 by 8 (12.5 years) ignores compounding. The rule is an approximation that works best for moderate rates.

questions.q: Which of the following cash equivalents is covered by FDIC deposit insurance, up to the applicable limits?
options: A certificate of deposit issued by an FDIC-member bank
Commercial paper issued by a large corporation
Shares of a money market mutual fund
A 13-week Treasury bill
questions.explain: FDIC insurance protects deposits at member banks, such as checking accounts and CDs. Money market fund shares are securities, not deposits, and are not FDIC insured even when sold at a bank. Treasury bills are backed by the U.S. government itself rather than by FDIC insurance, and commercial paper has no insurance at all.

questions.q: How do investors earn a return on U.S. Treasury bills?
options: They receive semiannual coupon payments
They receive monthly principal and interest payments
They receive a share of Treasury Department profits
They buy the bills at a discount and receive face value at maturity
questions.explain: T-bills have maturities of one year or less and pay no coupon. They are sold below face value, and the difference between the purchase price and the face amount received at maturity is the investor's interest. Semiannual coupons are paid on Treasury notes and bonds.

questions.q: Which description best fits commercial paper?
options: Long-term secured bonds backed by company real estate
Bank deposits insured by the FDIC
Short-term, generally unsecured promissory notes issued by corporations, usually at a discount
Government-guaranteed notes issued by federal agencies
questions.explain: Commercial paper is short-term corporate debt used to fund working capital. It is typically unsecured, backed only by the issuer's credit, and sold at a discount like T-bills. It is not a bank deposit and carries no FDIC insurance or government guarantee.

questions.q: How do Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS) protect investors against inflation?
options: The coupon rate is reset every month to match the inflation rate
The principal is adjusted for changes in the CPI, and the fixed coupon rate is paid on the adjusted principal
They are exempt from federal income tax when inflation is high
They pay a fixed dollar amount of interest regardless of inflation
questions.explain: With TIPS the coupon rate stays fixed, but the principal rises with the CPI. Because interest is computed on the adjusted principal, interest payments rise too. The coupon rate itself is not reset, and the inflation adjustments are subject to federal income tax.

questions.q: How is the interest on U.S. Treasury notes and bonds taxed for an individual investor?
options: Subject to federal income tax but exempt from state and local income tax
Exempt from federal tax but subject to state tax
Exempt from all income taxes
Subject to federal, state and local income taxes
questions.explain: Interest on Treasury securities is federally taxable, but states and localities may not tax it. This is the reverse of most municipal bonds, whose interest is generally exempt from federal tax, which is the trap answer.

questions.q: What is the main difference between a general obligation (GO) municipal bond and a revenue bond?
options: A GO bond is federally guaranteed, while a revenue bond is not
Revenue bonds are always safer than GO bonds
GO bond interest is taxable, while revenue bond interest is tax-exempt
A GO bond is backed by the issuer's taxing power, while a revenue bond is repaid from the income of a specific project
questions.explain: GO bonds rely on the full faith, credit and taxing authority of the issuing government. Revenue bonds are paid only from a defined source, such as tolls or utility fees, so their safety depends on that project. Neither type is federally guaranteed, and both are usually tax-exempt.

questions.q: A client in the 30% federal tax bracket is considering a municipal bond yielding 3.5%. What taxable yield would provide the same after-tax income?
questions.explain: Tax-equivalent yield = municipal yield / (1 - tax rate) = 3.5% / (1 - 0.30) = 3.5% / 0.70 = 5.0%. Multiplying 3.5% by 1.30 (4.55%) is a common error, and 2.45% is the after-tax yield of a taxable 3.5% bond.

questions.q: Interest rates drop sharply. What usually happens to holders of mortgage-backed pass-through securities?
options: Payments stop until rates rise again
Homeowners refinance, so principal comes back faster and must be reinvested at lower rates
The securities lengthen in maturity
The issuer must raise the coupon
questions.explain: Falling rates prompt homeowners to refinance and prepay their mortgages. Investors receive principal earlier than expected and have to reinvest it at the new lower rates, which is prepayment risk. Extension risk, where maturities lengthen, happens when rates rise.

questions.q: Which mortgage-backed securities carry the explicit full faith and credit guarantee of the U.S. government?
options: Ginnie Mae (GNMA) securities
Fannie Mae (FNMA) securities
Freddie Mac (FHLMC) securities
Private-label mortgage securities issued by banks
questions.explain: Ginnie Mae is a government agency, and its guarantee is backed by the full faith and credit of the United States. Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac are government-sponsored enterprises; their securities carry the enterprise's own guarantee, not an explicit federal one. Private-label pools have no government guarantee.

questions.q: Which is an example of an asset-backed security?
options: A Treasury bond
A general obligation municipal bond
A share of common stock
A bond secured by a pool of auto loans
questions.explain: Asset-backed securities are paid from the cash flows of a pool of receivables, such as auto loans, credit card balances or student loans. Treasuries and GO bonds are backed by governments, and common stock is equity, not a claim on a pool of loans.

questions.q: A corporation issues debentures. What backs these bonds?
options: A first mortgage on the company's buildings
A portfolio of securities held in trust
The general credit of the issuer, with no specific collateral
Equipment pledged to the bondholders
questions.explain: A debenture is unsecured debt. Holders rely on the company's overall ability to pay and rank behind secured creditors in a liquidation. Bonds backed by real estate are mortgage bonds, by securities collateral trust bonds, and by equipment equipment trust certificates.

questions.q: A callable bond (callable at par) is purchased at a premium. Which of its yields will be the LOWEST?
options: Yield to maturity
Yield to call
Current yield
Nominal (coupon) yield
questions.explain: For a premium bond the order from highest to lowest is nominal yield, current yield, yield to maturity, yield to call. The premium is lost over a shorter period if the bond is called, so yield to call is lowest. For a discount bond the order reverses.

questions.q: A bond with a $1,000 face value and a 6% coupon is trading at $960. What is its current yield?
questions.explain: Current yield = annual interest / market price = $60 / $960 = 6.25%. The 6% figure is the nominal coupon rate based on face value. A bond selling below par has a current yield above its coupon rate.

questions.q: Which bond would experience the largest price change if market interest rates rose by 1 percentage point?
options: A 20-year bond with an 8% coupon
A 2-year bond with a 3% coupon
A 6-month Treasury bill
A 20-year zero-coupon bond
questions.explain: Price sensitivity grows with duration. Longer maturity and lower coupons both raise duration, and a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity. A 20-year zero therefore has the highest duration of the choices. A high coupon returns cash sooner, which lowers duration.

questions.q: A bond portfolio has a duration of 7 years. If interest rates rise by 1 percentage point, what is the approximate change in the portfolio's value?
options: An increase of about 7%
A decline of about 1%
A decline of about 7%
A decline of about 0.7%
questions.explain: Duration estimates the percentage price change for a 1-point change in yield: -7 x 1% = about -7%. Prices move opposite to rates, so a rise in rates lowers value. The estimate is approximate because convexity is ignored.

questions.q: Under Standard & Poor's rating scale, which is the lowest rating category still considered investment grade?
options: BB
BBB
A
B
questions.explain: S&P investment-grade categories run from AAA down through BBB. Bonds rated BB and below are speculative, often called high-yield or junk bonds. Moody's equivalent cutoff is Baa. Many institutions are restricted to investment-grade holdings.

questions.q: An issuer is most likely to call its outstanding callable bonds when:
options: Interest rates have fallen well below the bonds' coupon rate
Interest rates have risen sharply
The issuer's credit rating has been lowered
The bonds are trading at a deep discount
questions.explain: Calling bonds lets the issuer refinance at lower rates, just as a homeowner refinances a mortgage. That happens when rates fall. Bondholders then face reinvestment risk. When rates rise, the bonds trade at a discount and calling them would make no financial sense.

questions.q: A $1,000 convertible bond can be converted into common stock at $40 per share. The stock is trading at $44. What is the bond's conversion value?
questions.explain: Conversion ratio = $1,000 / $40 = 25 shares. Conversion value = 25 x $44 = $1,100. If the bond trades below that amount, an arbitrage opportunity exists. The $1,000 figure is the face value, not the value of the shares received on conversion.

questions.q: A U.S. investor holds a bond issued by the Japanese government and denominated in yen. Which risk does the investor face that a holder of a U.S. Treasury bond does not?
options: Interest rate risk
Inflation risk
Currency risk if the yen weakens against the dollar
Reinvestment risk
questions.explain: Interest, inflation and reinvestment risk affect both bonds. Only the foreign bond exposes the investor to exchange rates: if the yen falls against the dollar, each yen payment converts into fewer dollars, lowering the investor's return.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a preemptive right for common stockholders?
options: To let holders sell shares back to the company at a fixed price
To let existing holders keep their proportionate ownership when the company issues new shares
To guarantee a minimum dividend
To give holders priority over bondholders in liquidation
questions.explain: Preemptive rights protect against dilution by giving current shareholders the first opportunity to buy new shares in proportion to their holdings. They do not create a put to the company, a dividend guarantee or a liquidation priority; common stock ranks last in liquidation.

questions.q: A company has 6% cumulative preferred stock with a $100 par value. It skipped preferred dividends for the past two years. Before it may pay a common dividend this year, how much must it pay per preferred share?
options: $0, because missed dividends are forgiven
questions.explain: Each year's dividend is 6% x $100 = $6. Cumulative preferred accumulates unpaid dividends in arrears, so the company owes 2 x $6 in arrears plus $6 for the current year = $18 before common holders receive anything. Forgiveness applies only to noncumulative preferred.

questions.q: Compared with straight (nonconvertible) preferred stock of the same issuer, convertible preferred usually:
options: Pays a higher dividend, because it is riskier
Has no par value
Ranks behind common stock in liquidation
Pays a lower dividend, because holders receive the option to convert into common stock
questions.explain: The conversion feature has value, so investors accept a lower dividend in exchange for the chance to share in common stock gains. Convertible preferred still ranks ahead of common stock in liquidation, and it typically has a stated par value.

questions.q: Which statement about American Depositary Receipts (ADRs) is correct?
options: They eliminate currency risk because they are priced in dollars
They are issued directly by the U.S. Treasury
They trade in the U.S. in dollars, but holders still bear currency risk from the underlying foreign shares
They give holders no right to receive dividends
questions.explain: ADRs are receipts issued by U.S. depositary banks for shares of foreign companies. Although quoted in dollars, their value tracks the foreign shares, so changes in exchange rates still affect returns. Dividends are converted into dollars and passed through to holders.

questions.q: An investor acquired restricted stock in a private placement from a company that has been an SEC reporting company for several years. Under SEC Rule 144, what minimum holding period applies before the shares may be resold publicly?
options: One year
Six months
Two years
There is no holding period
questions.explain: For an issuer that has been subject to Exchange Act reporting for at least 90 days, Rule 144 requires a six-month holding period for restricted securities. If the issuer is not a reporting company, the holding period is one year. Other conditions, such as public information, may also apply.

questions.q: How does the tax treatment of incentive stock options (ISOs) differ from nonqualified stock options (NSOs) at the time of exercise?
options: NSO exercise creates ordinary income on the spread, while ISO exercise creates no regular income tax but the spread may count for AMT
Both create ordinary income at exercise
ISO exercise creates ordinary income, while NSO exercise creates none
Neither has any tax consequence until the options expire
questions.explain: With NSOs, the difference between market value and exercise price is taxed as ordinary income when exercised. ISOs avoid regular tax at exercise, and if holding requirements are met the later gain is long-term capital gain, but the spread is an adjustment for the alternative minimum tax.

questions.q: An analyst studies price charts, moving averages, trading volume and support and resistance levels to time purchases. What type of analysis is this?
options: Fundamental analysis
Credit analysis
Discounted cash flow analysis
Technical analysis
questions.explain: Technical analysts study market data such as price patterns and volume, assuming that supply and demand show up in the charts. Fundamental analysts study the business itself, including earnings, balance sheets, management and industry conditions, to estimate intrinsic value.

questions.q: Which activity is MOST characteristic of fundamental analysis?
options: Plotting a stock's 200-day moving average
Tracking the advance-decline line
Comparing a company's earnings growth, margins and debt with others in its industry
Measuring short interest as a market sentiment gauge
questions.explain: Fundamental analysis looks at financial statements, competitive position, management and economic conditions to judge what a company is worth. Moving averages, advance-decline lines and short interest are market statistics used by technical analysts.

questions.q: A stock is expected to pay a $2.00 dividend next year, dividends are expected to grow 4% a year indefinitely, and investors require a 9% return. Using the constant-growth dividend discount model, what is the stock's value?
questions.explain: Value = next year's dividend / (required return - growth rate) = $2.00 / (0.09 - 0.04) = $2.00 / 0.05 = $40. Dividing by the required return alone ($2 / 0.09 = $22.22) ignores growth. The model only works when the required return exceeds the growth rate.

questions.q: Which statement best describes valuing a business by discounted cash flow?
options: The value equals the present value of the cash flows the business is expected to generate in the future
The value equals the book value of its assets
The value equals last year's net income times ten
The value equals the current market price of its shares
questions.explain: Discounted cash flow analysis projects future cash flows and discounts them at a rate reflecting risk. The sum is the estimated intrinsic value, which can then be compared with the market price. Book value and simple earnings multiples are different, cruder approaches.

questions.q: A company that went public three years ago sells additional new shares to the public. How is this offering best described?
options: An initial public offering
A private placement
A stock split
A secondary offering of new shares that dilutes existing holders
questions.explain: An IPO is a company's first sale of shares to the public. Later public sales are secondary (follow-on) offerings. When the company itself issues new shares, the share count rises and existing holders are diluted. When existing holders sell, the proceeds go to them, not the company.

questions.q: Which description best fits a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC)?
options: An operating company with a long earnings history
A mutual fund that invests in IPOs
A shell company that raises money in an IPO in order to buy a business it has not yet identified
A government agency that guarantees new issues
questions.explain: A SPAC, a type of blank check company, has no operations when it goes public. Investors are betting on management's ability to find and complete an acquisition, so the risks include an unknown target, dilution and the chance that no deal is completed.

questions.q: Which statement about closed-end funds is correct?
options: They continuously issue and redeem shares at net asset value
They issue a fixed number of shares that trade on exchanges and may sell at a premium or discount to net asset value
They must trade at exactly their net asset value
They cannot use leverage
questions.explain: Closed-end funds raise money in an offering and then their shares trade in the secondary market, where supply and demand set the price. That price can differ from NAV. Open-end mutual funds are the ones that continuously issue and redeem shares at NAV.

questions.q: An investor submits an order to redeem shares of an open-end mutual fund at 11 a.m. At what price will the redemption be made?
options: The next net asset value calculated after the order is received
The previous day's closing net asset value
The highest NAV of the day
A price negotiated with a market maker
questions.explain: Mutual funds use forward pricing: purchases and redemptions are executed at the next NAV computed after the order arrives, usually at the market close that day. Using a stale prior-day price would let investors exploit known market moves.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of hedge funds?
options: They are registered investment companies sold to the general public
They must redeem shares daily at NAV
They are guaranteed against loss
They are private funds generally limited to wealthy or institutional investors and may use leverage and short selling
questions.explain: Hedge funds are privately offered pools, usually restricted to accredited or other qualified investors, with flexible strategies including leverage, derivatives and short sales. They often impose lock-up periods and charge performance-based fees. They are not guaranteed and do not offer daily redemption like mutual funds.

questions.q: Which risk is most characteristic of a private equity or venture capital fund?
options: Daily price swings from exchange trading
Inflation-indexed principal adjustments
Illiquidity, because capital is typically committed for many years with limited ability to withdraw
Mandatory daily redemptions
questions.explain: Private equity and venture funds invest in private companies and usually lock up investors' capital for long periods, often a decade. There is no exchange market for the interests. Their risks include illiquidity, uncertain valuations and the failure of young companies.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a unit investment trust (UIT)?
options: It is actively managed by a portfolio manager who trades daily
It holds a largely fixed portfolio that is not actively managed and terminates on a set date
Its shares trade only on stock exchanges at a premium or discount
It has no termination date and no redemption feature
questions.explain: A UIT buys a set portfolio and generally holds it until a stated termination date. There is no ongoing management. Units are redeemable with the sponsor or trust at net asset value, so the description of an actively managed or exchange-only vehicle is wrong.

questions.q: Why do the market prices of exchange-traded funds (ETFs) generally stay close to their net asset value?
options: Authorized participants can create or redeem large blocks of shares, which lets arbitrage close price gaps
The SEC sets the price each day
ETFs can only be traded once a day at NAV
The fund sponsor guarantees the price
questions.explain: ETF shares trade all day on exchanges. If the price drifts above or below the value of the underlying holdings, authorized participants create or redeem creation units and profit from the difference, pushing the price back toward NAV. No regulator or sponsor fixes the price.

questions.q: Which statement about non-traded real estate investment trusts (REITs) is generally correct?
options: They trade on major exchanges throughout the day
They are guaranteed by the FDIC
They are not allowed to own commercial property
They can be hard to sell, may carry high up-front fees and can be difficult to value
questions.explain: Non-traded REITs are not listed, so investors depend on limited redemption programs or an eventual liquidity event. They often charge substantial offering costs and report values infrequently. Exchange-listed REITs, by contrast, can be bought and sold during market hours.

questions.q: How are most dividends from a real estate investment trust (REIT) taxed to an individual investor?
options: As tax-free return of capital in all cases
As long-term capital gains regardless of holding period
Mostly as ordinary income, because they generally do not qualify for the lower qualified dividend rate
They are not taxable if reinvested
questions.explain: REITs avoid corporate tax by distributing most of their income, so their ordinary dividends usually are not qualified dividends and are taxed at ordinary rates. Parts of a distribution may be capital gain or return of capital, but not always. Reinvesting does not avoid tax.

questions.q: An investor plans to put a large lump sum into a mutual fund family and hold it for many years. Which share class is generally most cost-effective?
options: Class C shares, because they have no front-end load
Class A shares, because a large purchase qualifies for breakpoint discounts and ongoing fees are lower
Class B shares, because the sales charge is deferred
All classes cost the same over time
questions.explain: Class A shares carry a front-end load that is reduced at breakpoints for large purchases, and they typically have lower annual 12b-1 fees. Class C shares avoid an up-front charge but have higher ongoing fees, which add up over a long holding period, making them costlier for long-term investors.

questions.q: Which statement about Rule 12b-1 fees is correct?
options: They are paid out of fund assets to cover distribution and marketing costs
They are paid only when shares are redeemed
They are a one-time charge at purchase
They are paid by the fund manager, not shareholders
questions.explain: 12b-1 fees are ongoing charges deducted from fund assets and included in the expense ratio, used for marketing, distribution and sometimes shareholder servicing. A one-time charge at purchase is a front-end load, and a charge at redemption is a contingent deferred sales charge.

questions.q: A mutual fund holds securities worth $520 million and has liabilities of $20 million. It has 25 million shares outstanding. What is its net asset value per share?
questions.explain: NAV per share = (total assets - liabilities) / shares outstanding = ($520 million - $20 million) / 25 million = $500 million / 25 million = $20.00. Forgetting to subtract liabilities gives $20.80.

questions.q: A fund's net asset value is $19.00 and its maximum sales charge is 5% of the public offering price. What is the public offering price?
questions.explain: Sales charges are stated as a percentage of the offering price, so POP = NAV / (1 - sales charge) = $19.00 / 0.95 = $20.00. Adding 5% of NAV ($19.95) understates the load because the charge is based on the higher offering price.

questions.q: An adviser wants to evaluate a U.S. small-cap stock fund. Which benchmark is most appropriate?
options: The Dow Jones Industrial Average
The Russell 2000 Index
The Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Bond Index
The S&P 500 Index
questions.explain: A benchmark should match the fund's asset class and style. The Russell 2000 tracks small-capitalization U.S. stocks. The Dow and the S&P 500 measure large-company stocks, and the Aggregate index measures investment-grade bonds, so comparisons with them would be misleading.

questions.q: A mutual fund shareholder has all distributions automatically reinvested. The fund distributes a capital gain at year-end. How is the distribution treated for tax purposes?
options: It is taxable in the year distributed even though it was reinvested
It is tax-free because it was reinvested
It is taxed only when the shares are sold
It reduces the shareholder's cost basis
questions.explain: Fund distributions are taxable when paid, whether received in cash or reinvested. The reinvested amount buys new shares and adds to the investor's cost basis, which prevents double taxation when the shares are later sold. Reinvestment does not defer the tax.

questions.q: An investor buys 1 XYZ 50 call at a premium of 3. Ignoring commissions, what is the breakeven price for the stock at expiration?
questions.explain: A call buyer profits when the stock rises above the strike price by more than the premium paid: $50 + $3 = $53. Below $53 at expiration the investor loses part or all of the $300 premium. $47 (strike minus premium) is the breakeven for a put buyer.

questions.q: An investor buys 1 ABC 40 put at a premium of 2. What is the maximum possible gain on this position, ignoring commissions?
options: Unlimited
questions.explain: The put gains as the stock falls. The most it can fall is to zero, so maximum gain = (strike - premium) x 100 = ($40 - $2) x 100 = $3,800. Unlimited gain belongs to call buyers, and $200 is the maximum loss (the premium paid).

questions.q: XYZ stock trades at $57. A 50 call on XYZ is quoted at a premium of 9. How much of the premium is time value?
questions.explain: Intrinsic value of a call = stock price - strike = $57 - $50 = 7. Time value = premium - intrinsic value = 9 - 7 = 2. Time value reflects the chance of further gains before expiration and decays as expiration approaches.

questions.q: Which options position carries the risk of an unlimited loss?
options: Writing an uncovered (naked) call
Buying a call
Buying a put
Writing a covered call
questions.explain: The writer of a naked call must deliver stock at the strike price however high the market goes, so losses have no ceiling. Option buyers can lose only their premium. A covered call writer already owns the shares, so the obligation is covered.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a warrant?
options: A short-term right to buy new shares below market, given to existing shareholders
A contract obligating the holder to buy stock at a future date
An exchange-listed option written by an investor
A long-term right issued by a company to buy its stock at a set price, often attached to a bond or preferred issue
questions.explain: Warrants are issued by the company itself, usually have long lives and an exercise price above the market price at issuance, and are often used as sweeteners. Short-term rights below market describe a rights offering, and an obligation to buy describes a futures contract.

questions.q: Which is a key difference between futures and forward contracts?
options: Forwards trade on exchanges, while futures are private
Futures carry more counterparty risk than forwards
Futures are standardized, exchange-traded and marked to market daily, while forwards are private, customized agreements
Forwards are settled daily through a clearinghouse
questions.explain: Futures trade on regulated exchanges with standard terms, and a clearinghouse guarantees performance and settles gains and losses daily. Forwards are negotiated directly between two parties, so each side is exposed to the other's possible default, which is counterparty risk.

questions.q: Which statement about a limited partnership is correct?
options: Limited partners manage day-to-day operations
Limited partners' liability is generally limited to their investment, while the general partner manages the business and has unlimited liability
Income is taxed at the partnership level and again when distributed
Interests are typically highly liquid
questions.explain: Limited partners are passive investors whose losses are generally capped at what they put in. The general partner runs the business and bears unlimited liability. Partnerships pass income and losses through to partners without entity-level tax, and LP interests are usually illiquid.

questions.q: What is a key risk of an exchange-traded note (ETN) that does not exist with an exchange-traded fund holding the index stocks?
options: Credit risk of the issuing bank, because the ETN is an unsecured debt obligation
Interest rate risk on the underlying stocks
Market risk from the index
Tracking error caused by fund expenses
questions.explain: An ETN is a senior unsecured note that promises to pay the return of an index. It holds no portfolio, so if the issuer fails, holders are general creditors. An ETF owns the underlying securities, which are held for shareholders. Both are exposed to the index's market risk.

questions.q: An index rises 10% on Monday and falls 10% on Tuesday. A fund seeking twice the index's DAILY return starts at $100. Ignoring fees, what is the fund worth after Tuesday?
questions.explain: Monday: $100 x 1.20 = $120. Tuesday: $120 x 0.80 = $96, a 4% loss. The index itself went from 100 to 110 to 99, a 1% loss, so the fund lost far more than twice the index. Daily resetting causes this compounding effect, which makes such funds unsuitable for most buy-and-hold investors.

questions.q: What is the stated objective of an inverse (short) index fund?
options: To match the index return over any period
To protect principal while capturing index gains
To deliver the opposite of the index's return, typically over a single day
To deliver twice the index return over a year
questions.explain: Inverse funds aim to move opposite to their benchmark, usually for one day. They are used to hedge or bet on declines. Because of daily resetting, their returns over longer periods can differ substantially from the simple inverse of the index's return.

questions.q: A client is offered a 'principal-protected' structured note linked to a stock index. Which risk remains even if the client holds the note to maturity?
options: No risk at all, because principal is protected
The issuer's credit risk, because the protection depends on the issuer being able to pay
Only currency risk
Only the risk of rising dividends
questions.explain: Structured notes are debt of the issuing institution. The promise to return principal is only as good as the issuer's ability to pay, so a default could cause losses. These notes may also cap upside, be hard to sell before maturity and have complex tax treatment.

questions.q: Which statement about a traditional fixed annuity is correct?
options: The insurance company bears the investment risk and guarantees the credited rate
The contract owner bears the investment risk in a separate account
It is a security that must be registered with the SEC
Its value fluctuates with the stock market
questions.explain: In a fixed annuity the insurer invests through its general account and promises a minimum rate, so it carries the investment risk. Because of this, fixed annuities are insurance products, not securities. Variable annuities, by contrast, place the risk on the owner through separate account subaccounts.

questions.q: Why is a variable annuity treated as a security?
options: The insurer guarantees a fixed rate of return
It is backed by the FDIC
It pays a fixed dollar amount for life
The owner bears the investment risk because values depend on separate account subaccounts
questions.explain: In a variable annuity, payments and account values rise and fall with the performance of the chosen subaccounts, so the investment risk shifts to the contract owner. That makes it a security, and a person selling it needs both securities and insurance licenses.

questions.q: Which feature is typical of an equity-indexed (fixed indexed) annuity?
options: Direct ownership of the stocks in the index
Unlimited participation in index gains
A guaranteed minimum value with interest credited partly by reference to an index, subject to caps or participation rates
Full exposure to index losses
questions.explain: Indexed annuities credit interest based on index performance but limit the upside through caps, spreads or participation rates, while protecting against index losses. The owner does not own the index stocks or receive their dividends.

questions.q: A client owns a nonqualified deferred annuity bought with after-tax money and takes a partial withdrawal before annuitizing. How is the withdrawal generally taxed?
options: The withdrawal is entirely tax-free return of principal
Earnings come out first and are taxed as ordinary income
Earnings are taxed as long-term capital gains
Principal comes out first, tax-free
questions.explain: For deferred annuities, withdrawals are treated as coming from earnings first, and those earnings are taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains. Only after all earnings have been withdrawn is the after-tax principal returned tax-free. An additional tax can apply to early withdrawals.

questions.q: Which type of life insurance offers flexible premiums and an adjustable death benefit, with cash value credited at a rate set by the insurer?
options: Universal life
Term life
Whole life
Variable life
questions.explain: Universal life lets the owner vary premium payments and adjust the death benefit within limits, with cash value growing at an insurer-declared rate. Term life has no cash value, whole life has fixed premiums and guaranteed values, and variable life cash value depends on separate account performance.

questions.q: What distinguishes variable life insurance from whole life insurance?
options: It has no death benefit
It has no cash value
The premium changes every month with interest rates
Cash value is invested in separate account subaccounts and is not guaranteed
questions.explain: Variable life invests cash value in subaccounts chosen by the policyowner, so cash value rises and falls with markets and is not guaranteed. Whole life provides a guaranteed cash value invested through the insurer's general account. Variable life is a security and is sold with a prospectus.

questions.q: An investor buys physical gold bullion. Which statement is most accurate?
options: It pays a fixed annual dividend
It is insured by SIPC against price declines
It produces no income and its return depends entirely on price changes
Its price is fixed by the U.S. Treasury
questions.explain: Bullion generates no interest or dividends, and storage and insurance cost money, so the return comes only from price changes. Investors often hold gold as a hedge against inflation or currency weakness. No agency protects against price declines.

questions.q: An investor holds cryptocurrency in a self-custodied digital wallet. Which risk is specific to this arrangement?
options: The FDIC will reimburse any losses
If the private keys are lost, the assets may be permanently inaccessible
Prices are fixed by a central bank
The holdings pay guaranteed interest
questions.explain: Control of a crypto asset depends on its private key. Lose the key and there is usually no way to recover the asset, and theft is often irreversible. Digital assets are also highly volatile, are not FDIC insured and are not issued or priced by a central bank.

questions.q: A client runs a bakery as a sole proprietorship. Which statement about this business form is correct?
options: The owner is personally liable for business debts, and business profits are reported on the owner's personal return
The business pays corporate income tax and the owner pays tax again on dividends
The owner's liability is limited to the amount invested
The business must have at least two owners
questions.explain: A sole proprietorship is not separate from its owner. Profits flow to the owner's individual return, and creditors of the business can reach the owner's personal assets. Limited liability requires forming an entity such as a corporation or LLC.

questions.q: Which business entity's earnings are generally taxed at the entity level and then taxed again when paid to owners as dividends?
options: An S corporation
A general partnership
A single-member LLC taxed as a disregarded entity
A C corporation
questions.explain: A C corporation pays corporate income tax on its profits, and shareholders pay tax again on dividends, creating double taxation. S corporations, partnerships and default LLCs are pass-through entities whose income is taxed only once, on the owners' returns.

questions.q: An adviser opens an account for a trust. Which document is most important for confirming who may direct the investments and what they may buy?
options: The grantor's most recent tax return
A letter from a beneficiary
The trust agreement or a certification of trust showing the trustee's powers
The beneficiaries' account statements
questions.explain: Trustees act under the authority of the trust instrument, which names them and sets out their investment powers and limits. The adviser should rely on that document or a certification of it, not on a beneficiary's wishes, since beneficiaries do not control trust assets.

questions.q: A client says she cannot sleep when her portfolio drops, although she has a large pension, no debts and decades before she needs the money. How would an adviser best describe her situation?
options: Low capacity and high willingness to take risk
High capacity to take risk but low willingness (tolerance) to take risk
High capacity and high willingness to take risk
Low capacity and low willingness to take risk
questions.explain: Risk capacity is the financial ability to absorb losses, which her pension, lack of debt and long horizon support. Risk tolerance is the emotional willingness to accept volatility, which is low here. A suitable plan must respect both, often by educating the client and choosing a moderate allocation.

questions.q: A client will need $80,000 for a home down payment in 18 months. Which investment is most suitable for this money?
options: A short-term Treasury or money market fund
A small-cap growth stock fund
A 20-year corporate bond
A non-traded REIT
questions.explain: Money needed soon should be kept where principal is stable and liquid. Stocks can fall sharply over 18 months, long-term bonds can lose value when rates rise, and non-traded REITs may be impossible to sell when the cash is needed.

questions.q: A client refuses to sell a stock that has fallen 40%, saying he will wait until he 'gets back to even,' even though the company's outlook has worsened. Which behavioral bias does this best illustrate?
options: Herding
Overconfidence in stock picking
Recency bias
Loss aversion (the disposition effect)
questions.explain: Loss-averse investors feel losses more strongly than equal gains, so they hold losers too long to avoid locking in the loss, while often selling winners too early. Herding is following the crowd, and recency bias is overweighting recent events.

questions.q: After three strong years in the stock market, a client wants to move everything into stocks because 'that's what has been working.' Which bias is most evident?
options: Anchoring
Mental accounting
Recency bias
Loss aversion
questions.explain: Recency bias leads people to assume recent results will continue, prompting them to chase past performance. Anchoring is fixating on a reference number such as a purchase price, and mental accounting is treating money differently depending on its source or label.

questions.q: When gathering client information, what is the main advantage of a face-to-face interview over a written questionnaire?
options: It produces data that need no verification
It helps uncover qualitative factors such as attitudes, values and family concerns
It satisfies all customer identification requirements by itself
It eliminates the need for documentation
questions.explain: Questionnaires capture standardized facts efficiently, but conversation draws out goals, feelings about risk and life circumstances that clients may not write down. Information from either method should be documented and updated, and identity verification is a separate process.

questions.q: A client has assets of $1.4 million (including a $600,000 home) and liabilities of $350,000 (including a $300,000 mortgage). What is the client's net worth?
questions.explain: Net worth = total assets - total liabilities = $1,400,000 - $350,000 = $1,050,000. The home and mortgage are included on a personal balance sheet. Excluding the home from assets but keeping all liabilities would wrongly give $450,000; subtracting only the home gives $800,000.

questions.q: The risk-free rate is 3%, the expected market return is 9%, and a stock's beta is 1.5. Under the capital asset pricing model (CAPM), what is the stock's expected return?
questions.explain: CAPM: expected return = risk-free rate + beta x (market return - risk-free rate) = 3% + 1.5 x (9% - 3%) = 3% + 9% = 12%. Multiplying beta by the full market return (13.5%) forgets to use the market risk premium.

questions.q: According to the semi-strong form of the efficient market hypothesis, which approach should NOT consistently produce above-average risk-adjusted returns?
options: Trading on material nonpublic information
Holding a low-cost index fund
Analyzing published financial statements
Taking more systematic risk
questions.explain: The semi-strong form says prices already reflect all public information, so neither technical analysis nor fundamental analysis of public data should beat the market consistently. Only inside information (illegal to trade on) could help. Taking more market risk may raise expected returns, but not risk-adjusted returns.

questions.q: If markets are efficient in the weak form only, which analysis cannot be used to earn consistent excess returns?
options: Fundamental analysis of company earnings
Technical analysis of past prices and volume
Analysis of inside information
Analysis of economic data
questions.explain: Weak-form efficiency means past price and volume information is already in current prices, so chart patterns cannot predict future moves. Under weak form alone, fundamental and inside information might still give an edge. Stronger forms of the hypothesis rule those out as well.

questions.q: Under modern portfolio theory, what is the efficient frontier?
options: The set of portfolios offering the highest expected return for each level of risk
The set of portfolios with the lowest fees
A list of stocks with the highest past returns
The line showing returns of the risk-free asset
questions.explain: Modern portfolio theory combines assets based on their expected returns, volatilities and correlations. Portfolios on the efficient frontier cannot be improved: no other mix gives more return for the same risk or less risk for the same return. Portfolios below it are inefficient.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: What best describes tactical asset allocation?
options: Setting long-term target weights and rebalancing to them regardless of forecasts
Buying an index fund and never rebalancing
Choosing investments based only on a client's values
Temporarily shifting away from long-term target weights to exploit expected short-term market opportunities
questions.explain: Strategic allocation sets long-term targets based on the client's objectives and risk. Tactical allocation makes deliberate, short-term deviations from those targets to take advantage of perceived market conditions, then returns to the strategic mix.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: A $1,000,000 portfolio targets 60% stocks and 40% bonds. After a rally it holds $700,000 in stocks and $300,000 in bonds. What trade restores the target mix?
options: Sell $300,000 of stocks
Buy $100,000 of stocks
Sell $100,000 of stocks and buy $100,000 of bonds
Sell $40,000 of bonds
questions.explain: Target stock value = 60% x $1,000,000 = $600,000, and target bonds = $400,000. Moving $100,000 from stocks to bonds restores 60/40. Rebalancing sells assets that have grown overweight and buys those that have shrunk, keeping risk in line with the plan.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: Which approach is the clearest example of passive portfolio management?
options: Rotating among sectors based on economic forecasts
Holding a low-cost fund that tracks a broad market index
Buying stocks with low price-to-earnings ratios that the manager believes are underpriced
Timing the market with technical signals
questions.explain: Passive management aims to match an index's return at low cost instead of trying to beat it. Sector rotation, security selection based on valuation and market timing are all active strategies that rely on the manager's forecasts.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: A portfolio manager favors stocks with low price-to-earnings and price-to-book ratios and above-average dividend yields. Which style is this?
options: Value
Growth
Momentum
Capital appreciation through small-cap speculation
questions.explain: Value investors look for companies priced cheaply relative to earnings, book value or dividends, expecting the market to recognize their worth. Growth investors accept higher valuations for companies with faster expected earnings growth, and momentum investors buy what has been rising.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: A manager overweights utilities and consumer staples as the economy appears headed into a recession, planning to shift toward cyclical stocks when recovery looks likely. What technique is this?
options: Dollar-cost averaging
Indexing
Strategic asset allocation
Sector rotation
questions.explain: Sector rotation moves money among industries according to the stage of the business cycle, favoring defensive sectors such as utilities and staples in slowdowns and cyclical sectors in recoveries. It is an active technique, unlike indexing or fixed strategic targets.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: An investor invests $600 each month in a fund for three months, buying at $10, $15 and $20 per share. What is the investor's average cost per share?
options: About $13.85
questions.explain: Shares bought: 60 + 40 + 30 = 130. Total invested: $1,800. Average cost = $1,800 / 130 = about $13.85, below the $15 average price. Dollar-cost averaging buys more shares when prices are low. It does not guarantee a profit or protect against loss in a declining market.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: An investor owns 1,000 shares of a stock and writes 10 covered calls on them. What is the main effect of this strategy?
options: It eliminates all downside risk
It generates premium income but caps the upside if the stock rises above the strike price
It creates unlimited upside
It doubles the dividend income
questions.explain: Writing covered calls brings in premium, which slightly cushions a decline, but the shares may be called away if the price rises above the strike, limiting gains. The investor still bears nearly all the downside risk of owning the stock.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: A client with a large gain in a stock wants protection against a sharp decline over the next few months while keeping the upside. Which strategy best fits?
options: Buying put options on the stock (a protective put)
Selling call options on the stock
Buying more shares on margin
Selling the stock short against the box and buying calls
questions.explain: A protective put gives the right to sell at the strike price, setting a floor on losses while leaving the upside open, at the cost of the premium. Writing calls limits upside and offers little protection. Buying on margin increases risk rather than reducing it.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: An investor buys a stock using 50% margin. If the stock rises 20%, what is the approximate return on the investor's own equity, ignoring interest and costs?
questions.explain: With 50% margin, the investor controls $2 of stock for each $1 of equity. A 20% rise in the stock's value produces a gain equal to 40% of the equity. Leverage magnifies losses the same way, and margin interest reduces the net result.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: An investor builds a bond ladder with equal amounts maturing every year for ten years. What is the main benefit?
options: It eliminates credit risk
It guarantees the highest possible yield
It spreads interest rate and reinvestment risk across maturities and provides regular liquidity
It concentrates holdings in a single maturity
questions.explain: Because some bonds mature every year, the investor can reinvest at prevailing rates or use the cash, avoiding a bet on one rate environment. A ladder does not remove credit risk, and concentrating in one maturity describes a bullet strategy.

questions.ref: 2.3 Portfolio management strategies, styles and techniques
questions.q: Which statement best describes high-frequency trading?
options: A long-term buy-and-hold strategy
Computer algorithms execute very large numbers of orders in fractions of a second to capture tiny price differences
Rebalancing a portfolio once a year
Placing orders through a human floor broker
questions.explain: High-frequency traders use automated programs, fast connections and short holding periods, often seconds or less, to profit from small spreads and price discrepancies. It is the opposite of buy-and-hold investing and is generally used by specialized firms, not individual clients.

questions.q: An investor bought shares on March 10 of one year and sells them at a gain on March 10 of the following year. How is the gain classified?
options: Short-term, because the shares were not held for more than one year
Long-term, because the shares were held for one year
Long-term, because the sale occurred in a new calendar year
It is not taxable
questions.explain: A gain is long-term only if the asset is held MORE than one year. The holding period starts the day after purchase, so selling on the one-year anniversary is still short-term and taxed at ordinary rates. Waiting one more day would make it long-term.

questions.q: A single investor has $2,000 of capital gains and $12,000 of capital losses this year. How much of the net loss may offset ordinary income this year?
options: Nothing; capital losses only offset capital gains
$3,000, with the remaining $7,000 carried forward
questions.explain: Net capital loss = $12,000 - $2,000 = $10,000. An individual may deduct up to $3,000 of net capital loss against ordinary income per year ($1,500 if married filing separately). The remaining $7,000 carries forward to future years without expiring.

questions.q: An investor sells a stock at a loss on December 1 and buys the same stock back on December 20. What is the tax result?
options: The loss is fully deductible this year
The loss is permanently lost
The loss is disallowed as a wash sale and is added to the cost basis of the new shares
The loss becomes a long-term gain
questions.explain: Buying substantially identical securities within 30 days before or after a loss sale triggers the wash sale rule. The loss is not deductible now; it is added to the basis of the replacement shares, so the benefit is deferred, not destroyed.

questions.q: A client inherits stock that the deceased bought for $20,000; it was worth $90,000 on the date of death. What is generally the client's cost basis?
questions.explain: Inherited property generally receives a basis equal to its fair market value at the date of death, a step-up. If the heir sells at $90,000, there is little or no gain. Property received as a lifetime gift, by contrast, usually keeps the donor's original basis for figuring gains.

questions.q: A client's taxable income places her last dollars in the 24% bracket, but her total federal tax equals 16% of taxable income. Which rate should be used to evaluate the tax on an additional $1,000 of interest income?
options: 24%, the marginal rate
16%, the effective rate
The average of 16% and 24%
0%, because interest is tax-exempt
questions.explain: The marginal rate applies to the next dollar of income, so it is the right rate for comparing investments and estimating the tax on extra income. The effective rate is total tax divided by total income and reflects lower brackets already filled.

questions.q: Exercising incentive stock options and holding the shares can trigger which tax issue even though no regular income tax is due at exercise?
options: The wash sale rule
The kiddie tax
The estate tax
The alternative minimum tax
questions.explain: The spread between market price and exercise price on ISOs is an adjustment for the alternative minimum tax, a parallel tax system that limits certain benefits. Clients exercising large ISO grants should project AMT before acting.

questions.q: How are qualified dividends taxed for an individual investor?
options: At ordinary income rates in all cases
They are tax-exempt
At the lower long-term capital gains rates, if holding period requirements are met
At a flat 50% rate
questions.explain: Qualified dividends from U.S. corporations and many foreign companies receive the preferential long-term capital gains rates when the investor meets a minimum holding period around the ex-dividend date. Nonqualified dividends, such as most REIT dividends, are taxed as ordinary income.

questions.q: Why is retaining income inside a non-grantor trust often tax-inefficient compared with distributing it to beneficiaries?
options: Trust income is never taxed
Trusts reach the highest federal income tax bracket at a much lower level of income than individuals
Trusts pay tax only on capital gains
Distributions are taxed twice
questions.explain: Trust tax brackets are compressed, so even modest retained income can be taxed at the top rate. Distributed income generally carries out to beneficiaries, who report it at their own, often lower, rates. Distributions are not taxed twice.

questions.q: A married U.S. citizen leaves her entire estate outright to her U.S. citizen husband. How does this transfer generally affect federal estate tax at her death?
options: It qualifies for the unlimited marital deduction, so no estate tax is due on that transfer
It is fully taxable because spouses are treated like other heirs
It is taxable only above $1,000
The husband must pay gift tax on it
