questions.explain: Transfers between spouses who are U.S. citizens qualify for an unlimited marital deduction for estate and gift tax purposes. Tax may apply later at the surviving spouse's death. Different rules apply when the receiving spouse is not a U.S. citizen.

questions.q: Which statement about assets held in a revocable living trust is correct?
options: They are removed from the grantor's estate for estate tax purposes
They cannot be changed during the grantor's life
They must be distributed when the trust is signed
They generally avoid probate but are still included in the grantor's taxable estate
questions.explain: A revocable trust lets assets pass to beneficiaries without probate, but because the grantor keeps control and can revoke it, the assets remain in the grantor's estate. Removing assets from the taxable estate generally requires an irrevocable transfer.

questions.q: How are distributions from a traditional IRA funded entirely with deductible contributions generally taxed?
options: As long-term capital gains
Tax-free
As ordinary income
Only the earnings are taxed, at capital gains rates
questions.explain: Because contributions were deducted and growth was tax-deferred, every dollar withdrawn is taxed as ordinary income, regardless of whether the growth came from capital gains. Capital gains treatment does not apply inside IRAs.

questions.q: A 40-year-old has contributed $30,000 to a Roth IRA over several years; the account is now worth $45,000. Which withdrawal can she generally take free of income tax and of the additional tax on early distributions?
options: The full $45,000
Up to $30,000 representing her contributions
Only the $15,000 of earnings
Nothing until age 59 1/2
questions.explain: Roth IRA withdrawals come from contributions first, and regular contributions can be taken out at any time without tax or penalty. Earnings withdrawn before the account meets the five-year and age 59 1/2 (or other qualifying event) tests may be taxable and subject to the additional tax.

questions.q: A 50-year-old withdraws money from her traditional IRA to pay for a vacation; no exception applies. In addition to ordinary income tax, what applies?
options: A 10% additional tax on the taxable amount
A 50% excise tax
No additional tax, because she is over 50
A 20% capital gains tax
questions.explain: Distributions taken before age 59 1/2 are generally subject to a 10% additional tax on top of regular income tax unless an exception applies, such as death or disability. Reaching age 50 does not create an exception for a vacation withdrawal from an IRA.

questions.q: A self-employed consultant with no employees wants to make both employee deferrals and employer profit-sharing contributions to her own retirement plan. Which plan is designed for this?
options: A Coverdell education savings account
A 457(b) plan
A 403(b) plan
A solo (individual) 401(k)
questions.explain: A solo 401(k) covers a business owner with no employees other than a spouse. The owner contributes in two roles, as employee through deferrals and as employer through profit sharing. 403(b) plans are for schools and certain nonprofits, and 457(b) plans for governments and some tax-exempt organizations.

questions.q: Which employer can sponsor a 403(b) plan for its employees?
options: A publicly traded manufacturer
A sole proprietor with no employees
A public school district or a 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital
A partnership of attorneys
questions.explain: 403(b) plans are available to public educational institutions and organizations exempt under Section 501(c)(3), such as many hospitals and charities. For-profit businesses, partnerships and self-employed individuals use 401(k) plans or other arrangements instead.

questions.q: An executive participates in her employer's nonqualified deferred compensation plan. What is a key risk of this arrangement?
options: The plan must cover all employees equally
Deferred amounts are generally subject to the claims of the employer's creditors if the company becomes insolvent
Contributions are immediately taxable
It is protected by ERISA funding rules like a pension
questions.explain: Nonqualified plans can favor selected executives and defer taxes, but to keep that deferral the benefits usually remain unsecured promises of the employer. If the company fails, participants stand in line with general creditors. Qualified plans hold assets in trust for participants.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares a defined benefit pension plan with a defined contribution plan?
options: In a defined benefit plan the employer bears the investment risk of providing the promised benefit
In a defined benefit plan the employee chooses investments and bears the risk
Defined contribution plans promise a fixed monthly benefit
Defined benefit plans have individual account balances
questions.explain: A defined benefit plan promises a formula-based benefit, so the employer must fund the shortfall if investments disappoint. In a defined contribution plan, such as a 401(k), the benefit depends on contributions and investment results in each participant's account, and the employee bears the risk.

questions.q: A participant leaving a job asks for her 401(k) balance to be paid to her by check so she can roll it into an IRA herself. What applies to this indirect rollover?
options: No withholding applies, and she has one year to complete the rollover
The plan withholds 10%, and she has 30 days
The full amount is taxable regardless of what she does
The plan must withhold 20% for federal tax, and she has 60 days to complete the rollover
questions.explain: Eligible rollover distributions paid to the participant are subject to mandatory 20% withholding, and the rollover must be completed within 60 days. To roll over the full amount she must make up the withheld 20% from other funds. A direct trustee-to-trustee rollover avoids withholding.

questions.q: Under ERISA Section 404(c), what is the main benefit for a plan sponsor that lets participants direct their own investments among a broad range of options?
options: The sponsor no longer has any fiduciary duty at all
The plan becomes exempt from ERISA
Plan fiduciaries are generally relieved of liability for losses that result from participants' own investment choices
Participants are guaranteed against investment loss
questions.explain: If participants truly exercise control over their accounts and the plan meets the regulation's conditions, fiduciaries are not liable for losses caused by participants' choices. Fiduciaries remain responsible for prudently selecting and monitoring the menu of options offered.

questions.q: Which action by a pension plan trustee is most likely an ERISA prohibited transaction?
options: Buying a diversified index fund for the plan
Lending plan assets to the sponsoring employer
Paying reasonable fees to an unrelated custodian
Rebalancing the plan to its target allocation
questions.explain: ERISA bars most transactions between a plan and parties in interest, which include the sponsoring employer. Lending plan money to the employer is a classic prohibited transaction. Prudent investing and paying reasonable fees to unrelated service providers are normal fiduciary activities.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of an investment policy statement (IPS) for a retirement plan or client portfolio?
options: To document objectives, constraints, asset allocation and how investments will be monitored
To guarantee a minimum return
To replace the need for a written advisory contract
To disclose the adviser's disciplinary history
questions.explain: An IPS sets out goals, risk tolerance, time horizon, allowed investments and monitoring and rebalancing procedures. It guides decisions and shows that fiduciaries followed a prudent process. It does not guarantee performance or replace the advisory contract or disclosure documents.

questions.q: A grandparent opens a 529 college savings plan for a grandchild. Which statement is correct?
options: The grandchild controls the account at age 18
Contributions are deductible on the federal return
Withdrawals for any purpose are tax-free
Earnings are federally tax-free when used for qualified education expenses, and the account owner keeps control of the money
questions.explain: Qualified 529 withdrawals avoid federal tax on earnings, and the owner, not the beneficiary, controls the account and can change the beneficiary to another family member. Federal tax law gives no deduction for contributions, and earnings in nonqualified withdrawals are taxable and usually face an additional tax.

questions.q: Which statement about an account under the Uniform Transfers to Minors Act (UTMA) is correct?
options: The donor can take the money back at any time
The custodian may use the assets for the custodian's own expenses
The gift is irrevocable and the assets belong to the minor, who takes control at the age set by state law
The account may have several minors as beneficiaries
questions.explain: A gift to a custodial account is permanent. The custodian manages the assets for the benefit of one minor, who receives them on reaching the age of termination set by state law. Using the assets for the custodian's own purposes would be a breach of duty.

questions.q: Which condition must an individual meet to contribute to a health savings account (HSA)?
options: Be over age 65
Be covered by a high-deductible health plan
Be enrolled in an employer's flexible spending account
Have no earned income
questions.explain: HSA eligibility requires coverage under a qualifying high-deductible health plan and generally no other disqualifying coverage. Contributions are deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free. Unused balances carry over from year to year.

questions.q: A brother and sister own a brokerage account as joint tenants with right of survivorship. The brother dies. What happens to his interest?
options: It passes automatically to the sister, outside of probate
It passes under his will to his heirs
It goes to his estate and through probate
The account is frozen until a court divides it
questions.explain: With JTWROS, a deceased owner's interest passes by operation of law to the surviving owner, avoiding probate. Under tenants in common, by contrast, the deceased's share would go to his estate and be distributed under his will or state law.

questions.q: Three business partners own an investment account as tenants in common with unequal shares. One partner dies. What happens to her share?
options: It passes equally to the surviving owners
It reverts to the brokerage firm
It is divided among all three estates
It passes to her estate, not to the other owners
questions.explain: Tenants in common may hold unequal interests, and there is no right of survivorship. A deceased tenant's share becomes part of her estate and goes to her heirs or beneficiaries. Survivorship is the feature of joint tenancy, which is the trap answer.

questions.q: Which statement about tenancy by the entirety is correct?
options: Any number of unrelated people can use it
Each owner can sell their share without the other's consent
It is available only to married couples and, where recognized, can protect the property from creditors of just one spouse
The deceased owner's share passes through probate
questions.explain: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of joint ownership for spouses, recognized in some states. It includes survivorship rights, and neither spouse can transfer or encumber the property alone, which in many states shields it from the separate creditors of one spouse.

questions.q: A client registers her brokerage account as transfer on death (TOD) to her son. Which statement is correct?
options: Her son becomes a co-owner immediately
She keeps full control during her life, and the account passes to her son at her death without probate
Her son must consent to every trade
The account must go through probate before her son receives it
questions.explain: TOD and payable on death registrations name a beneficiary who receives the assets at the owner's death, bypassing probate. The beneficiary has no rights while the owner is alive, and the owner can sell assets or change the beneficiary at any time.

questions.q: A client's will leaves everything to his children, but the beneficiary on file for his IRA is his former spouse. Who generally receives the IRA at his death?
options: The former spouse, because the beneficiary designation controls
The children, because the will controls
The estate, through probate
The IRA custodian
questions.explain: Retirement accounts and life insurance pass by beneficiary designation, outside the will. Unless the designation was changed or a state law or court order overrides it, the named beneficiary receives the assets. Clients should review designations after life events such as divorce.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a qualified domestic relations order (QDRO)?
options: To transfer an IRA between brokerage firms
To name a guardian for minor children
To appoint an executor for an estate
To let a qualified retirement plan pay part of a participant's benefit to a former spouse or other alternate payee
questions.explain: A QDRO is a court order, typically issued in a divorce, that directs a qualified plan to pay benefits to an alternate payee such as a former spouse. Without it, plans generally cannot assign benefits to someone other than the participant.

questions.q: A client contributes appreciated stock to a donor-advised fund this year but wants to recommend grants to charities over several years. What is the main tax advantage?
options: The deduction is spread over the years in which grants are made
The client keeps legal control of the assets
The client can generally take the charitable deduction in the year of the contribution, even though grants are made later
The grants are deductible a second time when paid
questions.explain: Contributions to a donor-advised fund are completed gifts to the sponsoring charity, so the deduction is generally available in the contribution year. The donor may recommend grants over time, but the sponsor has legal control. There is no second deduction when grants go out.

questions.q: A market maker quotes a stock at $25.10 bid and $25.20 ask. A customer places a market order to buy. At about what price will the order execute?
options: $25.10, the bid
$25.20, the ask
$25.15, the midpoint
Any price the customer chooses
questions.explain: The ask (offer) is the price at which the dealer will sell, so a buyer pays the ask. The bid is the price at which the dealer will buy from a seller. The $0.10 difference is the spread, a trading cost. Price improvement can occur, but the expected execution is near the ask.

questions.q: A customer who is short a stock at $50 wants to limit losses if the price rises. Which order should be placed?
options: A buy stop order above the current price
A sell stop order below the current price
A sell limit order above the current price
A buy limit order below the current price
questions.explain: A short seller loses when the price rises. A buy stop placed above the market becomes a market order to buy once the stop price is reached, covering the short and capping the loss. Sell stops protect long positions, and a buy limit below the market would not trigger on a rise.

questions.q: An investor places a sell stop order at $40 on a stock trading at $45. The stock trades down to $40. What happens?
options: The order is filled at exactly $40 or not at all
The order is canceled
The order becomes a limit order to sell at $45
The order becomes a market order and is executed at the next available price, which may be below $40
questions.explain: When the stop price is reached, a stop order turns into a market order. In a fast market the execution price may be lower than $40. To guarantee a minimum price, the investor would need a stop-limit order, which risks not being filled at all.

questions.q: Which statement about short selling stock is correct?
options: The maximum loss equals the sale proceeds
It can be done in a cash account
The seller borrows shares to sell and faces theoretically unlimited loss if the price rises
The short seller receives the dividends paid on the borrowed shares
questions.explain: A short seller sells borrowed shares, hoping to buy them back cheaper. Because a stock's price has no upper limit, losses are theoretically unlimited. Short sales must be done in a margin account, and the short seller must pay the lender any dividends declared.

questions.q: A broker-dealer sells a customer a bond out of its own inventory and adds a markup to the price. In what capacity is the firm acting?
options: As agent (broker)
As principal (dealer)
As custodian
As transfer agent
questions.explain: When a firm buys from or sells to customers from its own account, it acts as principal and is compensated through a markup or markdown. As an agent, it would arrange a trade between the customer and another party and charge a commission. Confirmations must disclose the capacity.

questions.q: Which description best fits a market maker?
options: A dealer that stands ready to buy and sell a particular security at publicly quoted prices on a regular basis
A firm that only holds client assets for safekeeping
A regulator that sets stock prices
An investment adviser that manages discretionary accounts
questions.explain: A market maker continuously quotes both a bid and an ask, trading from its own inventory and earning the spread, which adds liquidity. Holding assets is the custodian's role, and no regulator sets prices.

questions.q: A broker-dealer receives payments from a wholesaler for routing customer orders to it. What is this practice called and what is the main concern?
options: Soft dollars; it is always prohibited
A markup; it is illegal for listed stocks
Front running; it is permitted with consent
Payment for order flow; it can create a conflict with the duty of best execution, so it must be disclosed
questions.explain: Payment for order flow is compensation for directing orders to a particular venue. It is legal but creates an incentive that may conflict with seeking the best execution for customers, so firms must disclose it and still meet their best execution obligations.

questions.q: What does a broker-dealer's duty of best execution require?
options: Always executing at the lowest commission
Executing every order on the same exchange
Using reasonable diligence to obtain the most favorable terms reasonably available for the customer's order
Guaranteeing the customer a profit
questions.explain: Best execution looks at price and other factors, such as speed, likelihood of execution and market conditions, to get the most favorable result reasonably available. The lowest commission alone does not satisfy the duty if the execution price is worse.

questions.q: A customer buys $20,000 of stock in a new margin account. Under the current Regulation T initial requirement, how much must the customer deposit?
questions.explain: Regulation T currently requires initial margin of 50% for most equity securities: 50% x $20,000 = $10,000. The broker lends the other $10,000. FINRA's $2,000 minimum equity applies to opening a margin account, but here the 50% requirement is higher.

questions.q: A customer has a long margin account with a $10,000 debit balance. Using FINRA's 25% minimum maintenance requirement, below what market value would a maintenance call be issued?
options: About $13,333
questions.explain: Equity must be at least 25% of market value, so the debit can be at most 75% of market value. Market value at the threshold = $10,000 / 0.75 = about $13,333. At that point equity is $3,333, which is 25% of $13,333. Firms may set higher house requirements.

questions.q: In the U.S. securities markets, what is the main role of a qualified custodian such as a bank or broker-dealer?
options: Setting interest rates
Choosing investments for clients
Approving securities offerings
Holding and safeguarding client securities and cash and reporting holdings
questions.explain: Custodians keep client assets in safekeeping, settle trades, collect income and send statements. Advisers make investment decisions, and regulators review offerings. Using an independent qualified custodian helps protect clients against misappropriation.

questions.q: An investor buys a stock at $50, receives $2 in dividends and sells it a year later at $56. What is the holding period return?
questions.explain: Holding period return = (ending price - beginning price + income) / beginning price = ($56 - $50 + $2) / $50 = $8 / $50 = 16%. Leaving out the dividend gives 12%, which understates total return.

questions.q: An investment returned a cumulative 21% over two years. What is its annualized (compound annual) return?
questions.explain: Annualized return = (1 + cumulative return)^(1/years) - 1 = (1.21)^(1/2) - 1 = 1.10 - 1 = 10%. Simply dividing 21% by 2 (10.5%) ignores compounding; 10% earned twice gives 1.10 x 1.10 = 1.21.

questions.q: A consultant is comparing portfolio managers whose clients added and withdrew money at different times. Which return measure is most appropriate?
options: Time-weighted return
Dollar-weighted (money-weighted) return
Current yield
Nominal return before fees
questions.explain: Time-weighted return removes the effect of client deposits and withdrawals, which managers do not control, so it measures the manager's skill. Dollar-weighted return is an internal rate of return influenced by the timing and size of cash flows, which fits measuring an individual investor's experience.

questions.q: Which return measure is essentially the internal rate of return of an account and is affected by the timing of the client's deposits and withdrawals?
options: Time-weighted return
Holding period return on a single share
Real return
Dollar-weighted return
questions.explain: The dollar-weighted (money-weighted) return finds the rate that equates all cash flows with the ending value, so adding money just before a strong period raises it. Time-weighted return links sub-period returns to strip out these flows.

questions.q: A bond fund earned a nominal return of 7% during a year when inflation was 3%. What was the approximate real return?
options: About 10%
About 2.3%
About 4%
About 7%
questions.explain: Real return is roughly nominal return minus inflation: 7% - 3% = about 4%. The precise figure is (1.07 / 1.03) - 1 = about 3.9%. Real return shows the gain in purchasing power.

questions.q: A client in the 25% tax bracket earns 6% on a fully taxable corporate bond. What is the after-tax return?
questions.explain: After-tax return = pretax return x (1 - tax rate) = 6% x 0.75 = 4.5%. The 1.5% figure is the tax taken, not the return kept. This calculation helps compare taxable bonds with tax-exempt alternatives.

questions.q: An analyst projects a 30% chance of a 15% return, a 50% chance of an 8% return and a 20% chance of a -5% return. What is the expected return?
questions.explain: Expected return = probability-weighted average = (0.30 x 15%) + (0.50 x 8%) + (0.20 x -5%) = 4.5% + 4.0% - 1.0% = 7.5%. Ignoring the negative sign on the third scenario would give 9.5%.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following is EXCLUDED from the definition of a broker-dealer?
options: A firm in the business of buying and selling securities for customers
A firm in the business of trading securities for its own account
An out-of-state firm with an office in the state that sells to retail clients
A bank
questions.explain: The Act's broker-dealer definition excludes agents, issuers, banks, savings institutions and trust companies, and certain out-of-state firms with no place of business in the state. A firm effecting trades for others or, as a business, for its own account fits the definition, and having an office in the state removes the out-of-state exclusion.

questions.q: A broker-dealer has no place of business in State X. Its only transactions in State X are with banks, insurance companies and other broker-dealers. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is its status in State X?
options: It must register in State X because it effects transactions there
It must register only if it earns commissions in State X
It is not a broker-dealer in State X and need not register there
It may do business there only after notifying the SEC
questions.explain: A firm with no place of business in the state that deals only with issuers, other broker-dealers or financial institutions and institutional buyers falls outside the state's broker-dealer definition. Institutional counterparties are presumed able to protect themselves, so registration is not required.

questions.q: A broker-dealer licensed only in Ohio, with no office in Florida, receives a call from an existing Ohio customer who is spending the winter in Florida and wants to buy stock. Under the Uniform Securities Act as amended by NASAA, may the firm accept the order without registering in Florida?
options: No, every transaction with a person in Florida requires Florida registration
Yes, because the customer is an existing customer whose residence is not in Florida
Yes, but only if the customer moves to Florida permanently
No, unless the customer is an institutional investor
questions.explain: The NASAA amendments exclude from the broker-dealer definition a firm with no place of business in the state that is licensed where it does have one, when it deals with an existing customer whose residence is not in the state. This accommodates clients who are only temporarily present, such as seasonal residents.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, if no denial order is in effect and no proceeding is pending, when does a broker-dealer's registration generally become effective?
options: At noon of the 30th day after the application is filed
Immediately upon filing
At the end of the 10th business day after filing
Only when the Administrator signs an approval order
questions.explain: Registration becomes effective at noon on the thirtieth day after a complete application is filed, unless the Administrator acts. The Administrator may set an earlier effective date or defer it after an amendment is filed. Registration is not automatic upon filing.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act as amended by NASAA, when does a broker-dealer or agent registration expire if it is not renewed?
options: One year from its effective date
On the anniversary of the firm's formation
Registrations never expire
On December 31
questions.explain: The NASAA amendment sets a uniform expiration date of December 31 for registrations and notice filings unless renewed, which supports annual renewal through the Central Registration Depository. A rolling one-year term was an earlier approach that the amendment replaced.

questions.q: A broker-dealer files to withdraw its state registration and no proceeding is pending or instituted. Under the Uniform Securities Act, which statement is correct?
options: Withdrawal is effective immediately and ends the Administrator's authority
Withdrawal takes effect only after a hearing
Withdrawal is effective 30 days after the application is received, but the Administrator may still start a revocation proceeding within one year after it becomes effective
The Administrator must approve the withdrawal within 10 days
questions.explain: Withdrawal generally becomes effective 30 days after the Administrator receives the request, or sooner if the Administrator allows. Even after withdrawal is effective, the Administrator keeps the power, for one year, to institute a revocation or suspension proceeding for willful violations, so leaving cannot be used to escape discipline.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, the registration of a broker-dealer automatically registers which of the following as agents?
options: Every employee of the firm, including clerical staff
Its partners, officers and directors, and persons in similar positions
All agents of its affiliated firms
No one; every individual must file separately
questions.explain: Because the firm's application already discloses information on its partners, officers and directors, their registration as agents is automatic with the firm's. Other individuals who act as agents must register separately. Clerical staff who do not effect transactions are not agents at all.

questions.q: Along with its registration application, what must a broker-dealer file with the state Administrator under the Uniform Securities Act?
options: A consent to service of process
A list of all customers in the state
Audited financial statements of each agent
A copy of every advertisement it plans to use
questions.explain: Applicants must file a consent appointing the Administrator to receive service of process in noncriminal suits arising under the Act, so they can be sued in the state even if they are located elsewhere. A consent filed with an earlier registration need not be filed again.
questions.rule: Uniform Securities Act of 1956, Sections 202(a) and 414(g)

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 3110, which statement about a member firm's supervisory obligations is correct?
options: Supervision is required only for agents who handle discretionary accounts
Agents may supervise themselves once they have five years of experience
Written supervisory procedures are optional for small firms
The firm must establish and maintain a system, including written procedures, reasonably designed to supervise each associated person's activities
questions.explain: FINRA Rule 3110 requires every member to have a supervisory system and written procedures reasonably designed to achieve compliance with securities laws and FINRA rules, with registered principals responsible for supervision. The duty covers all associated persons, regardless of experience or firm size. Under state law, failure to supervise is also a ground for discipline.

questions.q: Under federal law, which requirement may a state Administrator NOT impose on a broker-dealer if it differs from or adds to the SEC's requirements?
options: Registration of the firm in the state
Payment of a state registration fee
Net capital and books-and-records requirements
Registration of the firm's agents
questions.explain: The National Securities Markets Improvement Act bars states from imposing capital, custody, margin, financial reporting or recordkeeping requirements on broker-dealers that differ from or exceed SEC rules. States still register broker-dealers and agents, collect fees and enforce antifraud laws. The Uniform Securities Act reflects this by deferring to Section 15 of the Exchange Act.

questions.q: Under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which description best fits a market maker?
options: Any customer who trades frequently
A dealer that holds itself out as willing to buy and sell a particular security for its own account on a regular or continuous basis
A firm that underwrites new issues only
An investment adviser that manages mutual funds
questions.explain: A market maker is a dealer that regularly publishes or otherwise provides two-sided quotations and stands ready to trade in a security from its own inventory. Frequent trading by a customer does not make that customer a dealer, and underwriting is a separate role.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following can be an agent?
options: Only an individual
A corporation
A partnership
Any legal person, including a trust
questions.explain: The Act defines an agent as an individual (other than a broker-dealer) who represents a broker-dealer or issuer in effecting or attempting to effect purchases or sales. Firms such as corporations and partnerships can be broker-dealers, investment advisers or issuers, but never agents.

questions.q: An employee of a state turnpike authority sells the authority's revenue bonds to investors and receives a salary but no commissions. Under the Uniform Securities Act, is the employee an agent?
options: Yes, anyone who sells securities to the public is an agent
Yes, because revenue bonds are not exempt securities
No, but only if the bonds are sold to institutions
No, an individual representing an issuer in transactions in exempt government securities is excluded
questions.explain: Revenue bonds of a state agency are exempt securities. An individual representing the issuer in selling securities exempt under that clause is excluded from the agent definition and need not register. The antifraud provisions still apply to the employee's conduct.

questions.q: A manufacturing company's human resources officer offers the company's own stock to existing employees under an employee purchase program. She receives no commission or other pay for soliciting. Under the Uniform Securities Act, she is:
options: An agent who must register
A broker-dealer
Not an agent
An investment adviser representative
questions.explain: The agent definition excludes individuals who represent an issuer in transactions with the issuer's existing employees, partners or directors, provided no commission or other remuneration is paid for soliciting anyone in the state. Paying her for the sales would change the result.

questions.q: An agent moves from Broker-Dealer A to Broker-Dealer B in the same state. Under the Uniform Securities Act, who must promptly notify the Administrator?
options: Only the agent
The agent, Broker-Dealer A and Broker-Dealer B
Only Broker-Dealer B
Only Broker-Dealer A
questions.explain: When an agent begins or ends an association with a broker-dealer, both the agent and the firm must notify the Administrator. In a move between firms, that means the agent, the old firm and the new firm all have a reporting obligation.

questions.q: An agent is terminated by her broker-dealer and is not yet associated with another firm. What is the status of her agent registration in the meantime?
options: It is not effective while she is not associated with a registered broker-dealer or issuer
It remains fully effective until December 31
It remains effective for 90 days
It converts automatically to a broker-dealer registration
questions.explain: An agent's registration is tied to a particular broker-dealer or issuer. During any period in which she is not associated with one, her registration is not effective and she may not act as an agent until a new association is in place and reported.

questions.q: Which form is used to register an individual agent with FINRA and the states through the Central Registration Depository?
options: Form BD
Form ADV
Form U5
Form U4
questions.explain: Form U4 is the uniform application for registration of individuals and is updated when disclosure information changes. Form U5 reports the termination of an individual's association. Form BD registers broker-dealer firms, and Form ADV registers investment advisers.

questions.q: An associated person of Firm A wants to open a personal brokerage account at Firm B. Under FINRA Rule 3210, what must happen first?
options: Firm B must obtain approval from FINRA
The associated person must notify the state Administrator
The associated person must obtain prior written consent from Firm A
Nothing; associated persons may open outside accounts freely
questions.explain: FINRA Rule 3210 requires an associated person to get the employer's prior written consent before opening an account at another member firm and to disclose the employment to the executing firm. The employer can then request duplicate statements and confirmations to monitor trading.

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 2040, which payment may a member firm generally make?
options: Referral fees to an unregistered accountant for each client who opens an account
Continuing commissions to a retired registered representative under a bona fide written contract entered into before retirement
A share of commissions to an agent's unregistered assistant who solicits trades
Commissions to an agent whose registration has lapsed
questions.explain: FINRA Rule 2040 generally prohibits paying transaction-based compensation to persons who are not registered. One exception allows continuing payments to retired representatives under a contract made while they were registered, if they no longer solicit. Referral fees and payments to unregistered solicitors are prohibited.

questions.q: An agent located in State A telephones a prospect in State B and offers to sell a security. Under the Uniform Securities Act, where has the offer been made?
options: In both State A, where it originated, and State B, where it was directed and received
Only in State A
Only in State B
In neither state until the sale is completed
questions.explain: An offer is made in a state when it originates from that state or is directed to and received in that state. An interstate call therefore involves both states, and the agent and the firm must be registered (or exempt) in each.

questions.q: A bona fide financial newspaper published in New York with more than two-thirds of its circulation outside New York over the past year runs a broker-dealer's advertisement offering securities. Under the Uniform Securities Act, is this considered an offer made in New York?
options: Yes, any advertisement printed in the state is an offer in the state
Yes, because the paper is published in New York
Only if a New York resident buys the security
No, the Act treats such a publication as not making an offer in the state
questions.explain: The Act says an offer is not made in a state by a bona fide newspaper of general, regular and paid circulation that is either published outside the state or published in the state but has had more than two-thirds of its circulation outside it during the past twelve months.

questions.q: An applicant for agent registration has completed rigorous training and passed the required examinations but has no work experience. Under the Uniform Securities Act, may the Administrator deny registration solely because of the lack of experience?
options: Yes, at least two years of experience is required
Yes, the Administrator has unlimited discretion
No, not if the applicant is qualified by training or knowledge
No, experience is never considered
questions.explain: The Act lets the Administrator consider training, experience and knowledge, but it may not enter an order solely on the basis of lack of experience if the applicant is qualified by training, knowledge or both. It must also recognize that a supervised agent need not have a broker-dealer's qualifications.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which conviction gives the Administrator grounds to deny an agent's application?
options: A misdemeanor traffic violation within the past ten years
A felony conviction within the past ten years
Any arrest, even without conviction
A felony conviction more than twenty years ago
questions.explain: The Administrator may act against an applicant convicted within the past ten years of any felony or of a misdemeanor involving a security or the securities business. An unrelated misdemeanor such as a traffic offense, a mere arrest, or a conviction outside the ten-year window does not fall under this ground.

questions.q: An agent places frequent trades in a retired client's conservative account, generating large commissions while the account value declines. Which unethical practice does this describe?
options: Churning (excessive trading)
Front running
Selling away
Marking the close
questions.explain: Inducing trading that is excessive in size or frequency in light of the customer's resources and the character of the account is churning. The agent profits from commissions at the client's expense. Front running and marking the close involve trading ahead of orders or manipulating prices, and selling away involves off-book transactions.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: An agent learns that his firm is about to execute a large buy order for an institutional customer and buys the same stock for his own account first. What is this practice called?
options: Arbitrage
Hedging
Interpositioning
Front running
questions.explain: Front running is trading ahead of a customer's large order to profit from the price movement the order is expected to cause. It abuses confidential customer information and is prohibited. Arbitrage exploits price differences between markets, and hedging reduces risk.

questions.q: A customer tells her agent: 'Buy 500 shares of XYZ for me today, but use your judgment on the exact time and price.' The agent has no written discretionary authority. Under the NASAA Statement of Policy, may the agent execute this order?
options: No, any judgment by the agent requires written discretionary authority
Yes, but only if the customer signs a power of attorney afterward
Yes, discretion limited to time and price is not treated as discretionary authority requiring written approval
No, the agent must execute immediately at the market
questions.explain: The customer chose the security, the action and the quantity. Leaving only time and price to the agent is not considered discretion under the Statement of Policy. If the agent had chosen the security or the number of shares, prior written discretionary authority would be required.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: An agent buys a stock in a customer's account without the customer's permission because he is confident it will rise. The stock gains 20%. Which statement is correct?
options: Because the customer profited, no violation occurred
The trade was unauthorized and is an unethical practice regardless of the profit
It is permitted if the agent informs the customer within 30 days
It is permitted if the customer has a margin account
questions.explain: Executing a transaction for a customer without authorization is a dishonest or unethical practice. Whether the trade made or lost money does not matter. The agent needed either the customer's specific instruction or prior written discretionary authority.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: A trader repeatedly enters large buy orders he never intends to execute, cancels them before they fill, and meanwhile sells shares at the higher prices his orders helped create. What is this manipulative practice called?
options: Spoofing (or layering)
Arbitrage
Dollar-cost averaging
Best execution
questions.explain: Spoofing and layering involve placing orders to create a false impression of supply or demand, then canceling them after other traders react. The trader profits on the opposite side. Such orders are deceptive because they were never meant to be filled.

questions.q: Two traders arrange to buy and sell the same thinly traded stock to each other at the same time, size and price to make the stock look actively traded. What is this practice?
options: A bona fide agency cross transaction
Legitimate market making
Block trading
Matched orders, a form of market manipulation
questions.explain: Entering coordinated orders of the same size, time and price to create a false appearance of active trading is manipulation. Wash trades, which involve no change in beneficial ownership, are similar. A bona fide agency cross for real customers on both sides is permitted.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: A corporate officer tells a friend about an unannounced merger in exchange for a favor, and the friend buys the target's stock knowing the information was confidential. Which statement is correct?
options: Only the officer is liable because he did not trade
Only the friend is liable because he traded
Both the officer (tipper) and the friend (tippee) may be liable for insider trading
Neither is liable because the merger was eventually announced
questions.explain: Insider trading liability arises from trading on material nonpublic information in breach of a duty. An insider who tips for a personal benefit breaches that duty, and a tippee who knows or should know of the breach and trades is also liable. Later public announcement does not cure the violation.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the component obligations of SEC Regulation Best Interest?
options: Disclosure obligation
A duty to monitor every retail account continuously after each recommendation
Care obligation
Conflict of interest obligation
questions.explain: Reg BI's general obligation is satisfied by meeting four components: disclosure, care, conflict of interest and compliance. It applies at the time of a recommendation and does not by itself create a duty to monitor accounts on an ongoing basis, unless the broker-dealer agrees to provide monitoring.

questions.q: Regulation Best Interest protects 'retail customers.' Who is a retail customer for this purpose?
options: A natural person who receives a recommendation and uses it primarily for personal, family or household purposes
Any customer with less than $1 million in assets
Any corporation with fewer than 100 employees
Only customers over age 65
questions.explain: Reg BI defines a retail customer as a natural person, or a legal representative of one, who receives a recommendation from a broker-dealer and uses it primarily for personal, family or household purposes. There is no asset test, and businesses are not covered.

questions.q: What is the purpose of Form CRS (the customer or client relationship summary)?
options: To register a broker-dealer with the SEC
To report suspicious transactions
To approve a customer for options trading
To give retail investors a short, plain-language description of services, fees, conflicts and disciplinary history
questions.explain: Form CRS is a brief disclosure that broker-dealers and SEC-registered advisers deliver to retail investors, explaining the relationship, services, fees and costs, conflicts of interest, standard of conduct and where to find disciplinary information, so investors can compare firms.

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 2111, which suitability obligation addresses whether a series of recommended trades is excessive when viewed together?
options: Reasonable-basis suitability
Customer-specific suitability
Quantitative suitability
Best execution
questions.explain: Quantitative suitability looks at the overall pattern of recommended transactions, such as turnover and cost, to ensure it is not excessive for the customer. Reasonable-basis suitability concerns the product or strategy in general, and customer-specific suitability concerns the individual investor's profile.

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 2121, how is the fairness of a markup on a principal trade with a customer judged?
options: By a fixed maximum percentage that applies to every trade
By all relevant circumstances, such as the security type, its availability, the price, the trade size and the expense of the trade
By the customer's net worth only
By whatever price the customer agrees to pay
questions.explain: FINRA expects markups to be fair and reasonable considering market conditions, the type and availability of the security, the price, the amount of money involved, the cost of executing the trade and disclosure. No single percentage is a safe harbor, and customer agreement does not make an excessive markup fair.

questions.q: Under the Section 28(e) safe harbor, which item may an investment manager obtain with client commission dollars (soft dollars)?
options: Research reports that assist in making investment decisions
Office rent for the manager's headquarters
Travel expenses for a marketing conference
Salaries of the manager's administrative staff
questions.explain: Section 28(e) of the Exchange Act protects managers who pay commissions for brokerage and research services that genuinely assist investment decision-making. Overhead such as rent, staff salaries and marketing travel benefits the manager rather than clients and falls outside the safe harbor.

questions.q: Under NASAA's policy statement on dishonest or unethical broker-dealer and agent practices, which action by an agent is prohibited?
options: Accepting a holiday card from a customer
Recommending a security that is suitable for the customer
Disclosing commissions to a customer
Borrowing money from a customer
questions.explain: The Statement of Policy lists lending money or securities to, or borrowing them from, a customer as an unethical practice for agents, together with acting as custodian of a customer's money or securities. Suitable recommendations and fee disclosure are proper conduct.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: Under the NASAA Statement of Policy, when may an agent share in the profits or losses of a customer's account?
options: Never under any circumstances
Whenever the customer agrees orally
Only with written authorization from both the customer and the broker-dealer the agent represents
Only if the account is a discretionary account
questions.explain: Sharing directly or indirectly in a customer's profits or losses is unethical unless the customer and the agent's broker-dealer have authorized it in writing. Oral consent is not enough, and discretionary status alone does not permit it.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: An agent sells shares of a private real estate venture to several clients without telling her broker-dealer, and the trades are not on the firm's books. What is this practice called?
options: Free riding
Selling away
Breakpoint selling
Interpositioning
questions.explain: Effecting securities transactions not recorded on the regular books of the agent's broker-dealer, unless the firm has authorized them in writing beforehand, is selling away. It deprives clients of the firm's supervision and is a dishonest or unethical practice.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: An agent assures a customer that the firm will make up any losses on a recommended stock. Under the NASAA Statement of Policy, this is:
options: An unethical practice, because it guarantees the customer against loss
Permitted if put in writing
Permitted if the stock is listed on an exchange
Permitted for accredited investors
questions.explain: Guaranteeing a customer against loss in a securities account or transaction is specifically listed as a dishonest or unethical practice. Putting the promise in writing or limiting it to certain customers does not make it acceptable.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: An agent who is not registered as an investment adviser representative puts the title 'Wealth Advisor' on her business card. Under the NASAA model rule on broker-dealer and agent practices as amended in 2025, this is:
options: Permitted, because 'advisor' is a generic word
Permitted if she has passed the Series 7
Permitted if the card also lists her broker-dealer
An unethical practice, unless otherwise permitted by law
questions.explain: The model rule treats using a title, credential or designation containing any variant of 'adviser' or 'advisor' without licensure as an investment adviser or investment adviser representative as unethical, unless otherwise permitted by law. Such titles suggest a fiduciary advisory relationship the agent cannot provide.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents

questions.q: A customer plans to invest $48,000 in a mutual fund whose next breakpoint is $50,000. The agent does not mention the breakpoint. Which statement is correct?
options: It is acceptable because the customer did not ask
It is acceptable because breakpoints are in the prospectus
Failing to tell the customer about the nearby breakpoint is an unethical practice
It is required, because breakpoints apply only to institutions
questions.explain: NASAA's statement of policy on investment company shares treats sales just below a breakpoint without disclosing the reduced charge available at a slightly higher amount as unethical. The agent should explain breakpoints, rights of accumulation and letters of intent so the customer can choose.
questions.rule: NASAA Statement of Policy on Dishonest or Unethical Business Practices of Broker-Dealers and Agents in Connection with Investment Company Shares

questions.q: Under the NASAA Model Act to Protect Vulnerable Adults from Financial Exploitation, what may a qualified individual at a broker-dealer do after reasonably believing an eligible adult is being financially exploited?
options: Close the account and keep the funds
Notify the state's adult protective services agency and the securities regulator, and delay a disbursement from the account
Notify the client's neighbors
Freeze all the client's bank accounts at other institutions
questions.explain: The model act encourages reporting suspected exploitation to adult protective services and the securities regulator, permits notifying a designated third party in certain cases, and allows a temporary delay of disbursements. Firms and individuals acting in good faith receive immunity. It does not authorize seizing or closing accounts.
questions.rule: NASAA Model Act to Protect Vulnerable Adults from Financial Exploitation

questions.q: Under the Uniform Prudent Investor Act, how is a trustee's investment decision evaluated?
options: In the context of the trust portfolio as a whole and as part of an overall strategy with suitable risk and return objectives
Investment by investment, with each holding judged in isolation
Solely by whether each investment made money
Only by whether the trustee avoided all stocks
questions.explain: The Act adopts modern portfolio theory ideas: no category of investment is inherently imprudent, diversification is generally required, and each decision is judged within the whole portfolio and overall strategy, based on facts at the time, not hindsight.

questions.q: A broker-dealer sells nondeposit investment products from a desk inside a bank branch. Under NASAA's rules for securities sales at financial institutions, what must customers be told?
options: The products are guaranteed by the bank
The products are insured because they are sold in a bank
Nothing, if the customer is already a bank depositor
The products are not FDIC insured, are not obligations of the bank and may lose value
questions.explain: Customers in bank branches may assume everything sold there is insured. The rules require clear disclosure that securities are not insured by the FDIC, are not deposits or obligations of the bank and involve investment risk, including possible loss of principal, plus separation of sales activity from deposit taking.
questions.rule: NASAA Rules for Sales of Securities at Financial Institutions

questions.q: A client who makes only one or two trades a year is placed in a wrap fee account that charges an annual percentage of assets. What is the main concern?
options: The client will be overcharged commissions on each trade
Wrap accounts may not hold mutual funds
The client may pay more than in a commission account, a problem sometimes called reverse churning
Wrap fees must be paid by the sponsor
questions.explain: A wrap fee bundles advice and execution into one asset-based fee. For an active trader it can be economical, but for a buy-and-hold client with little trading, paying the full wrap fee may cost more than paying commissions. Placing such clients in wrap programs can be unsuitable.

questions.q: Under SEC Rule 17a-4, how long must a broker-dealer preserve its blotters and general ledgers?
options: At least three years
At least six years, the first two in an easily accessible place
At least one year
Permanently
questions.explain: Rule 17a-4 requires blotters, general ledgers and customer account ledgers to be kept for not less than six years, the first two in an easily accessible place. Many other records, such as order tickets and communications, have a three-year requirement. Some organizational documents must be kept for the life of the firm.

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 2210, an agent emails the same market commentary to 20 retail investors over a two-week period. How is this communication classified?
options: Correspondence
Retail communication
Institutional communication
Research report requiring filing with FINRA
questions.explain: Correspondence is a written or electronic communication distributed to 25 or fewer retail investors within any 30-calendar-day period. Sending to more than 25 retail investors in that window would make it a retail communication, which generally requires principal approval before use.

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 2210, which statement about approval of communications is generally correct?
options: Correspondence must be approved by FINRA before use
No communication needs any review
Institutional communications must be filed with the state Administrator
Retail communications generally need a principal's approval before use, while correspondence is subject to supervision and review but not pre-approval
questions.explain: An appropriately qualified principal must approve most retail communications before they are used or filed. Correspondence and institutional communications are covered by supervisory procedures and review, often after the fact, rather than mandatory pre-approval.

questions.q: A broker-dealer's website ad states, 'Our recommended stocks will return at least 12% next year.' Under FINRA communication standards, this statement is:
options: Allowed if a footnote says past performance is no guarantee
Allowed if the firm's past returns exceeded 12%
Prohibited, because communications may not predict or project specific future performance
Allowed for accredited investors only
questions.explain: Communications must be fair and balanced and may not contain predictions or projections of performance, apart from narrow exceptions such as certain hypothetical illustrations. A promised minimum return is misleading, and a disclaimer does not cure it.

questions.q: When opening an account for a non-institutional customer, FINRA Rule 4512 requires the member to make reasonable efforts to obtain which of the following?
options: The customer's medical records
The name and contact information of a trusted contact person
A copy of the customer's will
The customer's credit card numbers
questions.explain: Rule 4512 requires basic account information, including the customer's name, residence, legal age and the associated person responsible, and reasonable efforts to get a trusted contact person. The trusted contact can be reached if the firm suspects exploitation or cannot reach the customer.

questions.q: Under FINRA Rule 2360, which step must occur before or at the time a customer's account is approved for options trading?
options: The customer must receive the options disclosure document
The customer must place a first trade
The customer must pass an exam
The customer must deposit $25,000
questions.explain: Options accounts must be approved by a qualified principal, and the options disclosure document explaining the characteristics and risks of standardized options must be furnished at or before approval. The firm also gathers financial information to judge suitability.

questions.q: Under SEC Regulation S-P, which requirement applies to broker-dealers and registered investment advisers?
options: Share customer data freely with any marketing firm
Obtain the SEC's approval before opening each account
Destroy all customer records after one year
Provide privacy notices and allow customers to opt out of certain sharing of nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties
questions.explain: Regulation S-P implements federal financial privacy law for SEC-regulated firms. It requires privacy notices, an opt-out right before sharing nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties (subject to exceptions), and written policies to safeguard customer records and information.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, when may the Administrator require a broker-dealer to file sales literature before use?
options: For every security, including U.S. Treasury bonds
Only for federal covered securities
For securities that are neither exempt nor federal covered securities
Never; sales literature is regulated only by FINRA
questions.explain: The Administrator may by rule or order require filing of prospectuses, advertisements and other sales literature, but not for exempt securities or transactions or for federal covered securities. Federal law preempts state review of materials for covered securities.

questions.q: Which statement best describes a tombstone advertisement for a securities offering?
options: A full sales brochure that replaces the prospectus
A limited announcement naming the issuer, security, price and underwriters, stating that the offer is made only by prospectus
A notice that a company has gone bankrupt
An advertisement guaranteeing the offering price
questions.explain: Tombstones are brief announcements permitted under SEC rules that identify the offering and where a prospectus can be obtained. They are not an offer to sell and cannot replace the prospectus, which is the document through which securities are actually offered.

questions.q: Under SEC Rule 10b-10, when must a broker-dealer send a customer a written confirmation of a transaction?
options: At or before completion of the transaction
Within 30 days after the trade
Only at the end of each quarter
Only if the customer requests one
questions.explain: Rule 10b-10 requires written notification at or before completion of the transaction (settlement), disclosing information such as the date, price, quantity, capacity in which the firm acted and, in many cases, compensation. Periodic statements do not replace confirmations.

questions.q: Under the Howey test, which set of elements makes an arrangement an investment contract (and therefore a security)?
options: Any purchase of property expected to rise in value
A loan repaid with fixed interest by a family member
Any contract signed before a notary
An investment of money in a common enterprise with an expectation of profits from the efforts of others
questions.explain: The Supreme Court in SEC v. W.J. Howey Co. defined an investment contract as an investment of money in a common enterprise, with an expectation of profits, derived from the efforts of a promoter or third party. Buying property one manages oneself lacks the reliance on others' efforts.
questions.rule: SEC v. W.J. Howey Co., 328 U.S. 293 (1946)

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following is NOT a security?
options: An investment contract
A certificate of interest in an oil and gas lease
A fixed annuity contract issued by an insurance company
A warrant to purchase common stock
questions.explain: The Act's definition expressly excludes insurance, endowment policies and annuity contracts under which an insurance company promises fixed payments. Investment contracts, interests in oil, gas or mining leases and warrants are all listed as securities. Variable annuities are securities because the owner bears the investment risk.

questions.q: An issuer files a registration statement with the SEC and wants to register the same offering in a state. Which method of state registration is designed for this situation?
options: Registration by qualification only
Registration by coordination
No state registration is ever needed
Registration through FINRA
questions.explain: Registration by coordination lets an issuer that has filed under the Securities Act of 1933 register in the state using the federal prospectus. If the state conditions are met, including being on file for a minimum period with no stop order pending, the state registration becomes effective at the same moment as the federal one.

questions.q: A small company plans an offering only to residents of its home state and will not register with the SEC. Which state registration method generally applies?
options: Registration by qualification
Registration by coordination
Registration by filing with the SEC
Notice filing as a federal covered security
questions.explain: Any security may be registered by qualification, the most complete method, which becomes effective when the Administrator orders. It is typically used when there is no federal registration to coordinate with, such as an intrastate offering. Coordination requires a federal registration statement.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, for how long is a registration statement generally effective?
options: Five years
Until December 31 of the current year
Permanently once approved
One year from its effective date, or longer while the distribution continues
questions.explain: A registration statement is effective for one year from its effective date, or any longer period during which the issuer or underwriters are still distributing the securities, except while a stop order is in effect. Unlike firm registrations, it does not expire on December 31.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following is an exempt security?
options: Common stock of a startup that is not listed on any exchange
Units of a private real estate limited partnership
A revenue bond issued by a city's water authority
Notes of a corporation maturing in five years
questions.explain: Securities issued or guaranteed by the U.S., a state, a political subdivision or their agencies and instrumentalities, including revenue obligations, are exempt from state registration. Unlisted startup stock, private partnership units and corporate notes need registration or a transaction exemption.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act as amended by NASAA, commercial paper is an exempt security if it matures within nine months, is issued in denominations of at least $50,000 and:
options: Is guaranteed by the FDIC
Is rated in one of the three highest categories by a nationally recognized statistical rating organization
Is sold only to residents of the issuer's state
Pays interest monthly
questions.explain: The exemption covers short-term notes, drafts, bills of exchange or bankers' acceptances maturing within 9 months, issued in denominations of at least $50,000 and rated in one of the 3 highest categories by a nationally recognized rating organization. Commercial paper is not insured by the FDIC.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which transaction is exempt from state securities registration?
options: An offer directed to no more than ten noninstitutional persons in the state in 12 months, where buyers purchase for investment and no commission is paid for soliciting them
Any sale by an issuer to the public through an underwriter
Any sale over $1 million
A sale to 50 retail investors solicited by telephone
questions.explain: The private placement exemption covers offers to not more than ten persons in the state (excluding institutions) during any twelve consecutive months, if the seller reasonably believes the buyers are purchasing for investment and no commission is paid for soliciting them. Public offerings to retail investors are not exempt.

questions.q: An investor calls his broker-dealer and, without any recommendation, asks to buy shares of an unregistered, non-exempt security that trades over the counter. Under the Uniform Securities Act, the trade is:
options: Prohibited because the security is not registered
Exempt only if the investor is an institution
A private placement
An exempt unsolicited nonissuer transaction
questions.explain: A nonissuer transaction effected by or through a registered broker-dealer under an unsolicited order is an exempt transaction. The Administrator may require the customer to acknowledge in writing that the order was unsolicited. The broker-dealer and agent must still be registered.

questions.q: A company offers securities under Rule 506 of Regulation D. What may a state Administrator require?
options: Full registration by qualification
Merit review of the offering terms
A notice filing, a consent to service of process and a fee
Nothing at all
questions.explain: Rule 506 offerings are federal covered securities, so states cannot require registration or review their merits. Federal law preserves state authority to require notice filings, consent to service of process and fees, and to pursue fraud.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which of the following involves an 'offer' or 'sale' of a security?
options: A bona fide pledge of stock as loan collateral
A purported gift of assessable stock
A stock dividend for which shareholders give nothing of value
A shareholder class vote on a merger
questions.explain: The Act treats a purported gift of assessable stock as an offer and sale, because the recipient may have to pay assessments. Bona fide pledges or loans, stock dividends where nothing of value is given, and acts incident to a class vote on a merger are expressly excluded from the definitions of offer and sale.

questions.q: A customer bought an unregistered, non-exempt security from an agent and still owns it. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what may the customer recover in a civil suit?
options: The price paid plus interest, costs and reasonable attorneys' fees, less income received, upon tendering the security
Triple damages plus punitive damages
Only the difference between the purchase price and today's price
Nothing, because the agent did not commit fraud
questions.explain: Selling a security in violation of the registration requirement creates civil liability whether or not there was fraud. A buyer who still holds the security may tender it and recover the consideration paid, plus interest, costs and reasonable attorneys' fees, minus any income received. Triple damages are not provided.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is the time limit for a buyer to sue for a violation of the Act's civil liability provisions?
options: Five years after the sale
One year after the sale, regardless of discovery
There is no time limit
Three years after the sale or two years after discovering the violation, whichever comes first
questions.explain: Suits under the civil liability section must be brought within three years after the contract of sale (or the rendering of advice) or within two years after discovering the facts constituting the violation, whichever occurs first. Waiting beyond either limit bars the claim.

questions.q: A seller who violated the Act makes a written offer to refund a buyer's purchase price plus interest, less income received, while the buyer still owns the security. The buyer ignores it. What is the result?
options: The buyer keeps the right to sue for three years regardless
The seller must double the refund
If the buyer fails to accept within 30 days of receiving the offer, the buyer may not sue under the Act
The offer has no legal effect
questions.explain: A rescission offer that meets the Act's terms cuts off the buyer's civil claim if the buyer, owning the security, does not accept within thirty days of receiving it. This lets sellers correct violations by making buyers whole.

questions.q: An agent materially aided a broker-dealer's sale of securities by means of misleading statements. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is the agent's civil exposure?
options: The agent has no liability because only the firm made the sale
The agent is jointly and severally liable with the seller unless the agent proves lack of knowledge despite reasonable care
The agent is liable only for commissions earned
The agent is liable only if criminally convicted
questions.explain: Control persons, partners, officers, directors, employees and broker-dealers or agents who materially aid the violation are liable jointly and severally to the same extent as the seller. The defense is proving they did not know, and with reasonable care could not have known, of the facts.

questions.q: A new client agreement contains a clause in which the client waives any rights under the state securities act. Under the Uniform Securities Act, this clause is:
options: Void
Valid if the client signs it
Valid only for accredited investors
Valid if approved by the Administrator
questions.explain: Any condition, stipulation or provision binding a person acquiring a security or receiving investment advice to waive compliance with the Act or its rules is void. Including such language can also be an unethical practice. Client signatures cannot waive statutory protections.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is the maximum criminal penalty for a willful violation of the Act?
options: A fine of $1 million and ten years in prison
Revocation of registration only
A fine of $500
A fine of $5,000, imprisonment for three years, or both
questions.explain: The model Act provides that a person convicted of a willful violation may be fined not more than $5,000, imprisoned not more than three years, or both. Revocation of registration is an administrative remedy, not a criminal penalty. Actual amounts can differ in states that adopted different figures.

questions.q: A person is convicted of willfully violating a rule adopted by the Administrator. Under the Uniform Securities Act, when can the person avoid imprisonment?
options: If the violation caused no losses
If the person pays a fine within 30 days
If the person proves he had no knowledge of the rule
Never; imprisonment is mandatory
questions.explain: The Act states that no person may be imprisoned for violating a rule or order if he proves he had no knowledge of it. A fine can still be imposed. The defense does not apply to violations of the statute itself.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, what may the state Administrator do when it appears a person is about to violate the Act?
options: Imprison the person directly
Issue a cease and desist order, with or without a prior hearing, or seek a court injunction
Impose criminal fines without going to court
Seize the person's personal bank accounts without a court order
questions.explain: The Administrator may issue a cease and desist order, with or without a prior hearing, and may ask a court for an injunction, receiver, rescission, restitution or disgorgement. Criminal penalties require prosecution in court, and the Administrator refers evidence to the appropriate prosecutor.

questions.q: During an investigation, a witness refuses to obey the Administrator's subpoena. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what can the Administrator do?
options: Apply to a court for an order requiring compliance, which can be enforced through contempt
Arrest the witness
Fine the witness without a hearing
Revoke the witness's driver's license
questions.explain: The Administrator can investigate inside or outside the state, administer oaths and subpoena witnesses and documents. If a person refuses to comply, the Administrator applies to the designated court, which can order compliance and punish disobedience as contempt.

questions.q: A broker-dealer wants a court to review a final order of the Administrator revoking its registration. Under the Uniform Securities Act, the petition must be filed within:
options: 10 days after entry of the order
One year after entry of the order
Three years after entry of the order
60 days after entry of the order
questions.explain: Any person aggrieved by a final order may seek review by filing a written petition in the designated court within sixty days after the order is entered. The court then reviews the Administrator's record, and findings of fact supported by competent evidence are generally conclusive.

questions.q: A SIPC-member brokerage firm fails while holding a customer's $400,000 of securities and $300,000 of cash, all missing. What is the maximum SIPC protection for this customer?
options: $500,000, of which no more than $250,000 may be for cash
questions.explain: SIPC protects up to $500,000 per customer in each separate capacity, including a $250,000 limit for cash. Here $400,000 of securities would be covered but only $100,000 of the cash fits within the $500,000 total, so $500,000 is the maximum. SIPC does not cover market losses.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, before the Administrator issues an order denying, suspending or revoking a registration (other than a summary postponement or suspension), what must generally be provided?
options: Only a phone call to the registrant
Prior notice, an opportunity for a hearing, and written findings of fact and conclusions of law
A jury trial
Approval by the SEC
questions.explain: Orders under Section 204 require appropriate prior notice (including to the employer of an agent), an opportunity for hearing, and written findings and conclusions. The only exception is a summary order postponing or suspending registration pending a final determination, after which a hearing is held on request.

questions.q: Under the Uniform Securities Act, which combination of factors makes a person an investment adviser?
options: Giving advice about securities, being in the business of doing so, and receiving compensation for it
Giving advice about any asset, even without pay
Selling securities on commission
Managing one's own portfolio actively
questions.explain: The definition covers persons who, for compensation, are in the business of advising others about the value of securities or the advisability of buying or selling them, or who issue securities analyses or reports as a regular business. Advice must concern securities, be given as a business and be compensated.

questions.q: A CPA prepares tax returns and also advertises 'personal investment management' services, charging a separate fee for stock recommendations. Under the Uniform Securities Act, the CPA is:
options: Excluded as an accountant in all cases
A broker-dealer
An agent of the clients
An investment adviser, because the advice is not solely incidental to the accounting practice
questions.explain: Lawyers, accountants, engineers and teachers are excluded only when their advice is solely incidental to their profession. Holding out investment advisory services and charging separately for them takes the CPA outside the exclusion, so registration as an investment adviser is required unless another exemption applies.

questions.q: A broker-dealer begins charging certain customers a separate annual fee for financial planning advice, in addition to commissions. Under the Uniform Securities Act, what is the consequence?
options: Nothing changes because broker-dealers are always excluded
The firm must give up its broker-dealer registration
The firm is no longer within the broker-dealer exclusion and must be registered as an investment adviser
Only the firm's agents must register as investment advisers
questions.explain: Broker-dealers are excluded from the adviser definition only when their advice is solely incidental to their brokerage business and they receive no special compensation for it. A separate advisory fee is special compensation, so the firm must register as an investment adviser as well.
